findings.title: Top view runs clockwise, mirroring the Moon's prograde orbit under a title that says "looking down"
findings.evidence: `const my = cy + r * Math.sin(moonAngle);` (main.ts:331) with no negation, and the same for both node dots (main.ts:338, 343). SVG y increases downward, so increasing ecliptic longitude moves the dot from 3 o'clock toward 6 o'clock — clockwise on screen. The panel title is `Top view (looking down on Moon's orbit)` (index.html:161). Looking down from the north ecliptic pole the Moon's orbital motion is counter-clockwise, so the drawing is the view from the SOUTH pole. The golden-reference demo uses the opposite, correct sign: moon-phases/logic.ts:183 `y: center.y - radius * Math.sin(angleRad)`, as does keplers-laws/main.ts:316 `cy - rAu * Math.sin(thetaRad) * scale`. CLAUDE.md states the rule and names this demo as unfixed: "a north-up (counter-clockwise) orbit needs cy - r*sin(theta). seasons and eclipse-geometry are still clockwise."
findings.scenario: A student clicks "Animate month" and watches the Moon travel clockwise around Earth with the Sun at the right. Reading the panel title literally, they conclude the Moon's orbital motion is retrograde and that the waxing crescent sits BELOW the Sun-Earth line. Having just used moon-phases, where the same top view runs counter-clockwise, they get two mutually mirrored pictures of the same orbit.
findings.fix:
Flip the geometry to agree with the golden reference (do NOT relabel the title to "south pole" — moon-phases ships an explicit "orbit motion" annotation showing CCW for the same orbit, so eclipse-geometry is the demo that is out of step):

1. apps/demos/src/demos/eclipse-geometry/main.ts — negate the y term at lines 331, 338, 344 and 363: `cy - r * Math.sin(...)` and `cy - labelR * Math.sin(angle)`. These are the only four `Math.sin` call sites in the file, so this is the complete in-panel inventory.

2. apps/demos/src/demos/eclipse-geometry/logic.ts:49 — `const dy = centerY - pointY;` so the drag inverse round-trips, and rewrite the docstring at lines 36-40, which currently advertises the clockwise convention as intentional and cites renderStage as its authority.

3. apps/demos/src/demos/eclipse-geometry/logic.ts:635-657 (buildArcPath) — negate both sin terms (y1, y2) AND change the main arc's sweep flag from 1 to 0, or all eight eclipse-window arcs will bulge the long way round the circle. The full-circle branch at 645-646 is sign-agnostic (two semicircles between (cx±r, cy)) and needs no change. Update its docstring at 631-633, which states "measured CW from 3-o'clock".

4. apps/demos/src/demos/eclipse-geometry/logic.test.ts:725-787 — rewrite the nine assertions that pin the CW convention (90 deg for a point directly below, 270 for directly above, 315 upper-right, 225 upper-left, 333.43 for the non-zero-centre case, and the round-trip loop that hard-codes `y = r*Math.sin(rad)`). Add the RED assertion the finding asks for: display longitude 90 deg must map ABOVE the centre line, y = -140 px at r = 140. Reading these assertions rather than their names is the point — they currently certify the defect.

5. Leave alone: buildBetaCurvePath (logic.ts:76, `panelCenterY - beta * yScale`) already negates correctly and matches its labelled +/- axis; flipping it would introduce a new upside-down graph. Also leave the betaLine (main.ts:378-382) and eclipseLabel (main.ts:302-304) screen-up offsets — out-of-plane is perpendicular to the screen in a top view, so screen-up is a convention either way. Just confirm no clipping now that the Moon can reach local y = -140 (absolute y = 80; the panel title sits at absolute y = 40, so it clears).

6. Then drop eclipse-geometry from CLAUDE.md:95, leaving "seasons is still clockwise", so the gotcha note stops naming a demo that has been fixed.

Not already fixed. `git log -5 -- main.ts` shows the last five commits touching it are sidebar/label, unicode-comment, speed-selector, UX-remediation and eclipse-reward work — none touches the sign. CLAUDE.md:95 reads verbatim "SVG y points down: a north-up (counter-clockwise) orbit needs `cy - r*sin(theta)`. seasons and eclipse-geometry are still clockwise." So the repo's own notes name this demo as an open item.

5. Cross-demo contradiction verified: moon-phases/logic.ts:183 is `y: center.y - radius * Math.sin(angleRad)` (CCW) and keplers-laws/main.ts:316 is `const py = cy - rAu * Math.sin(thetaRad) * scale` (CCW). moon-phases also ships an explicit `Show annotations (Sun direction / E-W / orbit motion)` toggle (moon-phases/index.html:195), so it asserts the orbit direction to the reader. A student who uses both demos is shown two mirror-image pictures of the same orbit, one of them labelled with the motion direction.

SEVERITY CORRECTED P0 -> P1, for reasons the finding does not weigh:
   - The convention is internally consistent across the whole panel and deliberately documented (logic.ts:36-40 "0 = right, angles increase clockwise (SVG y-down = positive). This matches renderStage()"; buildArcPath docstring logic.ts:631-633). Moon dot, both node dots, both node labels, all eight eclipse-window arcs (`buildArcPath`, sweep flag 1) and the drag inverse all share it. The picture is therefore a geometrically valid south-pole view, not a scrambled one: no eclipse window sits at the wrong elongation from the Sun direction, and no computed quantity is touched. Beta, the shadow-cone thresholds, node longitudes and the eclipse-type verdicts are all unaffected.
   - The second panel is already correct and must not be flipped: `buildBetaCurvePath` (logic.ts:76) is `const y = args.panelCenterY - beta * args.yScale`, which agrees with its labelled `+`/`-` axis (index.html:208-209).
   - `grep -ni "counter-clockwise|clockwise|prograde|eastward"` over the demo and its content file hits only code comments and test names — no reader-visible copy asserts a direction of motion. The only wrong reader-visible string is the title at index.html:161.
   - Readiness is honest, so no claim outruns its evidence: apps/site/src/content/demos/eclipse-geometry.md has `status: draft` (line 3) and `readiness: experimental` (line 10) with readinessReason "Core demo behavior is implemented, but parity and launch-gate signoff are still pending." None of the three stated learning goals (alignment/shadow geometry, umbra vs penumbra, why not every month) depends on handedness.
   So: a real, reachable, reader-visible convention defect and misleading copy that contradicts the golden reference and the project's own written rule — P1. It hardens to P0 the moment this demo is promoted past `experimental`, because the mislabelled viewpoint then becomes a verified public claim.

THE PROPOSED FIX IS RIGHT IN SUBSTANCE BUT INCOMPLETE AND MIS-CITED. Three of its four line references are wrong: `dy = pointY - centerY` is logic.ts:49 not :48; `placeNodeLabel`'s lx/ly are main.ts:362-363 not :365-366; `buildArcPath` is logic.ts:635-657 not :565-577. More importantly it omits the tests: logic.test.ts:725-787 contains nine assertions that PIN the clockwise convention (90 deg for a point directly below, 270 for directly above, 315 upper-right, 225 upper-left, 333.43 for the off-centre case, and a round-trip loop that hard-codes `y = r*Math.sin(rad)`). Applying the fix without rewriting them turns the suite red, and leaving them is exactly the repo's "tests encode the defect" failure mode. It also omits the two docstrings that advertise CW as intentional.

findings.title: During "Run simulation" state.moonLonDeg is never advanced, so the stage drawing and the phase/beta/outcome readouts are driven by a frozen Moon (phase drifts at -0.99 deg/day instead of +12.19) and stay stale after the run
findings.evidence: In the simulate branch the tick copies only two of three longitudes into state: `state.sunLonDeg = simulation.sunLonDeg; state.nodeLonDeg = simulation.nodeLonDeg; moonLon.value = String(simulation.moonLonDeg); render();` (main.ts:1241-1244). But `render()` ignores the slider while running: `const moonLonDeg = isAnimating ? state.moonLonDeg : clamp(Number(moonLon.value), 0, 360);` with `isAnimating = runMode !== "idle"` (main.ts:482-484), then writes `state.moonLonDeg = moonLonDeg` — i.e. itself. So `state.moonLonDeg` never advances for the whole run. The displayed phase angle is therefore norm(lambda_M_frozen - lambda_sun(t)), which drifts at -SUN_RATE = -360/365.2422 = -0.986 deg/day instead of +PHASE_RATE = +360/29.530588 = +12.19 deg/day: wrong sign and 12.4x too slow.
findings.scenario: A student runs the 10-year simulation (the fifth challenge requires it). The Moon dot sits still on the orbit while the two node dots sweep around it, and the Phase readout cycles New -> Waning -> Full backwards. The student concludes the eclipse seasons arise because the nodes move past a stationary Moon, and that the Moon's phase cycle runs the other way.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED by line-by-line trace plus independent recomputation. Severity corrected P0 -> P1.

1. The quoted code exists verbatim at the stated lines. apps/demos/src/demos/eclipse-geometry/main.ts:1241-1244 is exactly `state.sunLonDeg = simulation.sunLonDeg;` / `state.nodeLonDeg = simulation.nodeLonDeg;` / `moonLon.value = String(simulation.moonLonDeg);` / `render();` — no third `state.moonLonDeg` assignment. main.ts:481 `const isAnimating = runMode !== "idle";`, main.ts:484 `const moonLonDeg = isAnimating ? state.moonLonDeg : clamp(Number(moonLon.value), 0, 360);`, main.ts:490 `state.moonLonDeg = moonLonDeg;` — a self-assignment while running.

2. Control flow traced: `runMode = "simulate"` is set at main.ts:1493, so `isAnimating` is true for the whole run. I grepped every write to `state.moonLonDeg`: main.ts:490 (the self-assignment), 1192 (animate-month), 1207 (animate-year), 573 (state import), and tweenMoonTo (1387/1396/1405). None runs in the simulate branch. The slider is written programmatically at 1243, which fires no `input` event, so the listener at main.ts:1526 does not re-sync. So `state.moonLonDeg` is pinned at its pre-run value (set by the `render()` at main.ts:1468) for the entire run. Everything downstream of it is wrong: `getDerived({moonLonDeg: state.moonLonDeg, ...})` at main.ts:498, the `moonLonValue` readout at main.ts:516, and `renderStage({..., moonLonDeg, ...})` at main.ts:545.

3. Independent recomputation (my own `node -e`, not the finder's): sun = 360/365.2422 = 0.985647 deg/day; moon = 360/27.321661 = 13.176358 deg/day; node = -360/(18.61 x 365.25) = -0.052962 deg/day. Correct d(phase)/dt = moon - sun = 12.190711 deg/day, matching PHASE_RATE = 360/29.530588 = 12.190749 deg/day. Buggy d(phase)/dt = 0 - sun = -0.985647 deg/day. Ratio 12.3682. The finding's "wrong sign and 12.4x too slow" is right. Over 10 tropical years the phase readout should complete 123.7 cycles; it completes 10.00 backwards.

4. The defect is reachable and on a required path: challenge #5 (main.ts:932) is "Eclipse statistics: Run a simulation of at least 10 years", and `runSimulation` is only gated by `prefersReducedMotion` (main.ts:1463).

5. Not already fixed and not guarded. `git log -3` on the file: 7f51806, 9d35e40, 4fc1740 — none touches this. No guard exists. apps/site/tests/eclipse-geometry.spec.ts never clicks `#runSimulation` (only `#simYears`/`#simSpeed` option tests at spec:295-325), so nothing covers or encodes this path.

6. A persistent effect the finding missed: the completion block (main.ts:1256-1270) calls `stopLoop()` (which sets `runMode = "idle"` at main.ts:1039) but never calls `render()` again. The last frame was drawn while still "simulate", so after the run the `#moonLonValue` readout keeps the pre-run longitude while the `#moonLon` thumb sits at the final simulated longitude — two contradictory numbers on screen until the student touches a control.

7. A second effect the finding missed: `derived.betaDeg` comes from `eclipticLatitudeDeg(frozen moonLon, advancing nodeLon)`, so the `absBeta` readout and the beta indicator oscillate on the 360/0.052962 = 6797 d = 18.61 yr node period instead of the 27.212 d draconic period (360/(13.176358+0.052962)). The solar/lunar outcome readouts are likewise driven by a Moon that is not where the simulation has it.

Why P1 and not P0:
- The scientific deliverable is unaffected. `stepSimulation` (main.ts:1130-1137) advances `sim.sunLonDeg/moonLonDeg/nodeLonDeg` correctly and computes `phaseAngleDeg`, `betaDeg` and every eclipse count from `sim.*`, never from `state.*`. The results table the challenge actually asks the student to read is correct.
- The finder's failure scenario is wrong in its central visual detail. `renderStage` (main.ts:371-377) draws in a Sun-fixed frame, subtracting `sunLonDeg` from both the Moon and the node longitudes. Buggy Moon display rate = 0 - sun = -0.9856 deg/day; node display rate = node - sun = -1.0386 deg/day. They differ by only 0.0530 deg/day, so the Moon dot and the node dots regress nearly rigidly together — the Moon is not stationary and the nodes do not "sweep around it". The specific misconception claimed ("eclipse seasons arise because the nodes move past a stationary Moon") is not what is on screen.
- Legibility is limited. SIM_SPEED_DAYS_PER_SECOND (main.ts:1002-1006) is slow 200 / medium 2000 / fast 10000 days per second, so a 10-year run lasts 18.3 s / 1.83 s / 0.37 s. At medium and fast the stage is a blur with or without the bug (buggy Moon display rate -1971 deg/s and -9856 deg/s). Only at "slow" (-197 deg/s, a backwards cycle every 1.8 s) is the wrong direction perceptible.
So this is a real wrong drawing and real wrong readouts on an exposed, required path, with a stale-number state that persists after the run — but the physics engine and the reported statistics are correct, which puts it below "wrong number a student would believe".

findings.title: Spectrum tick and power-of-ten label rows are evenly spaced on an 18-decade log axis, misplacing every label by up to 72x and reading visible light as 31 nm
findings.evidence: index.html:100-108 emits seven tick spans (10 km, 1 m, 1 mm, 1 um, 1 nm, 1 pm, 10 fm) and style.css:125-131 lays them out as `grid-template-columns: repeat(7, minmax(0, 1fr))` with `text-align: center`, so label i is centred at (i+0.5)/7 of the bar width. The bar itself is linear in log10(lambda) from 1e6 cm to 1e-12 cm (logic.ts:96-97, 110-113). I recomputed both positions with node: true pos% = [0.00, 22.22, 38.89, 55.56, 72.22, 88.89, 100.00]; grid centres = [7.14, 21.43, 35.71, 50.00, 64.29, 78.57, 92.86]. The wavelength actually under each label is [5.18e+4, 1.39e+2, 3.73e-1, 1.00e-3, 2.68e-6, 7.20e-9, 1.93e-11] cm, i.e. ratios to the printed label of [0.052, 1.39, 3.73, 10.0, 26.8, 72.0, 19.3]. The `spectrum__powers` row (index.html:84-92) has the same defect and is worse-posed: its decade steps are 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, which cannot be equally spaced on any linear-in-log axis. The scale-objects row below the bar (main.ts:178-189) does use `wavelengthToPositionPercent`, so the same figure carries two mutually inconsistent axes.
findings.scenario: A student drags the marker until it sits above the tick labelled "1 nm" to find a 1 nm X-ray photon. The marker is actually at 26.8 nm, which this demo classifies as ultraviolet, and the readout panel says 26.8 nm while the axis says 1 nm. Reading the figure the way the figure invites costs almost 1.5 decades, and the error is not uniform, so no mental correction recovers it.
findings.fix:
Minimal honest fix, cheaper than the proposed one: change the labels, not the layout engine. On this axis a uniform 3-decade ladder is exactly equally spaced, so an edge-anchored CSS grid is already correct. I verified in node that 10^4, 10^1, 10^-2, 10^-5, 10^-8, 10^-11, 10^-14 m land at precisely 0, 16.667, 33.333, 50, 66.667, 83.333, 100% (and equivalently for the ticks row: 10 km, 10 m, 1 cm, 10 um, 10 nm, 10 pm, 10 fm = 1e6, 1e3, 1e0, 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9, 1e-12 cm). So:

1. Replace the seven label strings in index.html:84-92 and :101-107 with those uniform ladders, and change both CSS rules (style.css:61-67, :125-131) from `repeat(7, minmax(0,1fr))` + `text-align: center` to `repeat(7, minmax(0,1fr))` with `justify-items: center` plus `:first-child { justify-self: start }` and `:last-child { justify-self: end }` so the end labels sit flush with the bar's ends instead of being clipped. No JS, no absolute positioning, no height/collision problems.

2. Collapse the duplication while there: the two rows print the same seven wavelengths in cm-derived and SI form. Keep one row, derive it from a single exported `AXIS_TICKS: Array<{lambdaCm: number; label: string}>` in logic.ts, and render the SI form from the same array if the power-of-ten guide is pedagogically wanted.

3. Only if non-decade labels are genuinely required (e.g. marking 1 nm specifically), go the absolute route — but then also set an explicit `height` on each converted row (as style.css:139 does for `.spectrum__scale`), and anchor the ends with `transform: none` on the first and `translateX(-100%)` on the last rather than reusing `clamp(pos, 3, 97)` from main.ts:182, which would inject a fresh 0.54-dex error.

4. Add the unit test the finding asks for, but assert the contract rather than the CSS: for every entry in `AXIS_TICKS`, `wavelengthToPositionPercent(lambdaCm)` must equal the rendered left/justify position to within 0.01pp. That test only has teeth once the labels come from the shared array, which is the real architectural fix — one source of truth for the axis, already used by the gradient, marker, highlight and scale row.

5. Separately, give the axis to screen readers: both rows are `aria-hidden="true"`, so after this fix sighted students get a correct axis and non-sighted students still get none. An `aria-label` on `.spectrum` naming the range, or an sr-only list of the ticks, closes it.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED. I could not refute any part of this; my independent recomputation reproduces it exactly, and I found evidence that strengthens it.

1. CODE EXISTS AS QUOTED. `apps/demos/src/demos/em-spectrum/index.html:100-108` emits exactly seven tick spans (`10 km`, `1 m`, `1 mm`, `1 $\mu\mathrm{m}$`, `1 nm`, `1 pm`, `10 fm`), and `:84-92` emits the seven power-of-ten spans. `style.css:61-67` (`.spectrum__powers`) and `:125-131` (`.spectrum__ticks`) both set `grid-template-columns: repeat(7, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: 8px`, with `text-align: center` on the spans at `:69-71` and `:133-135`. Minor line drift in the finding: the axis constants are at `logic.ts:99-100` (`LAMBDA_MIN_LOG = log10(1e-12)`, `LAMBDA_MAX_LOG = log10(1e6)`) and the mapping at `:113-116`, not 96-97/110-113. Substance unaffected.

2. ARITHMETIC RE-DERIVED FROM SCRATCH (I converted each printed label to cm myself and reimplemented the mapping in node rather than reusing the finder's figures). Axis span = 18 decades, 1e6 cm at 0% to 1e-12 cm at 100%.
   - True positions: [0.00, 22.22, 38.89, 55.56, 72.22, 88.89, 100.00]%
   - Grid centres (i+0.5)/7: [7.14, 21.43, 35.71, 50.00, 64.29, 78.57, 92.86]% (the 8px gap shifts these by <0.5pp at a 700px bar, so it does not rescue anything)
   - Wavelength actually under each label: [5.179e+4, 1.389e+2, 3.728e-1, 1.000e-3, 2.683e-6, 7.197e-9, 1.931e-11] cm
   - Ratio actual/printed: [0.052, 1.39, 3.73, 10.0, 26.8, 72.0, 19.3]. Worst case 72x, at the tick printed "1 pm". Matches the finding to three figures.
   The `spectrum__powers` row is worse-posed as claimed: its decade steps are 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2 (10^4 -> 10^0 -> 10^-3 -> 10^-6 -> 10^-9 -> 10^-12 -> 10^-14 m), which cannot be equally spaced on any linear-in-log axis.

3. FULLY REACHABLE, NOTHING GUARDS IT. `main.ts:373-376` maps the slider (`index.html:22-30`, min 0 max 1000 step 1) linearly to bar position, `pos = value/1000*100`, then `positionPercentToWavelengthCm(pos)`. So the exposed control is a bar-position slider sweeping all 18 decades in 0.1% steps. `main.ts:206-207` places the marker via `wavelengthToPositionPercent`, `:214-218` the band highlight, `:182` the scale-objects row. The label rows are the only things off the true axis.

4. NOT FIXED, AND DEMONSTRABLY A KNOWN BUG CLASS LEFT HALF-FIXED. `logic.ts:93-101` carries a comment recording that this exact defect was already found and repaired for the gradient: hard-coded percentages "put red at 32% of an 18-decade log axis -- which is 1.74 cm, a radio wavelength," and "the bar and the marker disagreed about where 550 nm is by 13 percentage points." `spectrumGradientCSS()` now routes every colour anchor through `wavelengthToPositionPercent` (`logic.ts:266-275`). So the bar's colours were moved onto the true axis while the two label rows were left behind — the figure now carries three mutually inconsistent axes (colours + marker + scale row on the true axis, ticks and powers evenly spaced). `git log` on index.html/style.css shows the last touches were layout/a11y/chip work, nothing on tick placement.

5. NO TEST PINS IT, IN EITHER DIRECTION. `design-contracts.test.ts:121-122` only asserts the string `"spectrum__powers"` appears in the HTML; it never checks placement. `logic.test.ts:45-76` tests `wavelengthToPositionPercent` itself (which is correct) and never compares it to the rendered labels. So nothing catches this and nothing blocks the fix.

6. SEVERITY P0 UPHELD, with a sharper scenario than the finder's. Because the gradient is on the true axis, the rainbow paints at 56.42%-57.89% (I recomputed: 700 nm -> 56.42%, 380 nm -> 57.89%), whose centre at 57.15% falls at fraction 0.501 between the labels "1 $\mu$m" (50.00%) and "1 nm" (64.29%). Reading the figure the way the figure invites therefore places visible light at 10^(-4 + 0.501*(-3)) = 3.147e-6 cm = 31.5 nm, against the truth of 380-700 nm: a factor of 17 understatement that lands visible light in the extreme UV, in a demo whose first stated learning goal (`em-spectrum.md:15`) is "Order EM bands by wavelength and frequency." The error is non-monotonic in the ratio list above, so no mental correction recovers it. Mitigations exist but do not demote it: the marker carries its own correct label (`main.ts:209`) and the readouts are correct, so no computed number is wrong — but a mislabelled axis on the demo's only figure is squarely "a wrong drawing a student would believe."

7. NOT a readiness-honesty finding: `apps/site/src/content/demos/em-spectrum.md:3,10` are `status: beta` and `readiness: candidate`, so no launch-ready claim is outrunning its evidence. One wrinkle worth a line to Anna: the `readinessReason` at `:11` says "the spectrum colours now sit at the right wavelengths," which is true of the colours and false of the labels over them.

8. THE PROPOSED FIX IS DIRECTIONALLY RIGHT BUT INCOMPLETE IN THREE WAYS, each of which would bite on implementation. (a) Absolutely positioned children collapse their parent's height — `.spectrum__scale` only works because `style.css:139` gives it `height: 24px`; converting the two rows without explicit heights collapses them to zero and overlaps them with the bar. (b) Edge clipping: the first tick sits at exactly 0% and the last at exactly 100%, so `transform: translateX(-50%)` throws half of "10 km" off the left edge and half of "10 fm" off the right. Critically, the fix must NOT reuse the scale row's `clamp(pos, 3, 97)` from `main.ts:182` — on an 18-decade axis a 3% clamp is 0.54 dex, i.e. it would replace a large lie with a 3.5x one. (c) Even once positioned truly, "1 pm" (88.89%) and "10 fm" (100%) are 11.1% apart and will collide at phone widths, as will the two rows' labels with each other.

9. ONE MORE DEFECT THE FINDING MISSES: the two rows are the same seven wavelengths printed twice in two unit systems (a DRY violation, one table's worth of duplicated truth), and both are `aria-hidden="true"`, so screen-reader users get no wavelength axis at all. Fixing the geometry does not give them one.

findings.title: Microwave band is defined as 0.1-1 mm (submillimetre), so all four of its own listed examples - and the CMB peak - classify as Radio
findings.evidence: logic.ts:40-41 sets microwave lambdaMinCm = 1e-2 (0.1 mm), lambdaMaxCm = 1e-1 (1 mm), i.e. 300 GHz to 3.00 THz (computed), which is the submillimetre/terahertz band. logic.ts:44 lists `examples: "Microwave ovens, CMB, molecular clouds, radar"`. I computed each: a 2.45 GHz oven is lambda = 12.236 cm; 10 GHz radar is 2.998 cm; the CMB peak at T = 2.72548 K is lambda_max = b/T = 0.10632 cm = 1.063 mm; CO(1-0) at 115.271 GHz is 2.601 mm. Tracing bandFromWavelengthCm (logic.ts:180-196): each of these is > BANDS.microwave.lambdaMaxCm = 1e-1, so the function returns "radio" for all four. The conventional definition is 1 mm to 1 m (300 MHz to 300 GHz). The contradiction is explicit elsewhere too: logic.ts:33 lists "the cosmic microwave background" under Radio examples, and packages/data-spectra/src/emSpectrumObjects.ts:94-95 tags the CMB object `bands: ["Microwave"]`.
findings.scenario: A student clicks the Microwave chip. The marker jumps to bandCenterCm("microwave") = 316 um and the band card says microwave ovens, radar and the CMB live here. The student then drags to 12 cm to check the oven and the badge flips to Radio. They leave believing microwave ovens emit at 0.3 mm, two to three decades wrong, and that the CMB is not microwave.
findings.fix:
Move the band edges, then fix every surface that referred to the old placement, then make the overlap explicit in copy.

1. logic.ts:50-51 infrared -> `lambdaMinCm: 7e-5, lambdaMaxCm: 1e-1` (700 nm to 1 mm; this is the conventional IR span including far-IR/submm).
2. logic.ts:40-41 microwave -> `lambdaMinCm: 1e-1, lambdaMaxCm: 1e2` (1 mm to 1 m = 300 MHz to 300 GHz).
3. logic.ts:29-30 radio -> `lambdaMinCm: 1e2, lambdaMaxCm: 1e6` (1 m to 10 km).
   These three keep the contiguity invariant at logic.test.ts:459-462 satisfied.
4. Re-sort the examples/descriptions to match the new edges, which the finder's fix omits:
   - logic.ts:33-34 radio examples -> drop "WiFi" and "the cosmic microwave background" (both microwave now); keep AM/FM (1 MHz = 3e4 cm, 100 MHz = 300 cm) and radio galaxies; keep pulsars only with the note in (6), since pulsar observing spans 100 MHz-3 GHz and therefore straddles the boundary.
   - logic.ts:44 microwave examples -> "Microwave ovens, WiFi, radar, the CMB, cold molecular gas (CO)". All verified inside 1 mm-1 m by the numbers above.
   - logic.ts:53-54 infrared examples -> add a far-IR/submm item (e.g. "cold dust at 100-500 um, Herschel/SOFIA") so the newly widened band is honest about what now lives at its long end.
5. Fix the two tests that pin or mislabel the defect:
   - logic.test.ts:363-364: rename to "returns infrared for 0.3 mm" (0.03 cm is 0.3 mm, not 3 mm) and assert `"infrared"`, which is what the corrected edges give.
   - logic.test.ts:357: `bandFromWavelengthCm(21)` now returns "microwave". Change the assertion and name it so the reason is on the record, e.g. "21 cm HI sits in the microwave L-band by frequency (1.42 GHz) even though astronomers call it radio astronomy".
   - Add the discriminating cases the contiguity test cannot catch: `expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(12.2364)).toBe("microwave")` (2.45 GHz oven), `expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(0.10632)).toBe("microwave")` (CMB per-wavelength peak), `expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(0.26008)).toBe("microwave")` (CO 1-0), `expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(0.03)).toBe("infrared")` (300 um submm), `expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(300)).toBe("radio")` (100 MHz FM).
6. Add one sentence to BOTH band descriptions, because the partition is a teaching simplification and the demo should say so rather than imply microwave and radio are disjoint: in radio (logic.ts:31-32) and microwave (logic.ts:42-43), state that microwave is conventionally the short-wavelength end of the radio spectrum, that this demo splits them at 1 m so each wavelength gets one label, and that radio astronomy (the 21 cm line, pulsars, the VLA and ALMA) works on both sides of that split. Without this the 21 cm result in (5) will read as a new bug to the next reader.
7. Clean up the surfaces that are now consistent or still stale: logic.ts:246 `// 1 cm -- microwave` becomes correct, leave it; `packages/data-spectra/src/emSpectrumObjects.ts:94-96` CMB `bands: ["Microwave"]` becomes correct, leave it; re-read docs/audits/migrations/em-spectrum-parity.md and apps/site/src/content/instructor/em-spectrum/index.md for any quoted band range that names the old 0.1-1 mm microwave edges.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED on every point, independently recomputed.

1. Code exists as quoted. `/Users/anna/Teaching/cosmic-playground/apps/demos/src/demos/em-spectrum/logic.ts:40-41` is exactly `lambdaMinCm: 1e-2, // 0.1 mm` / `lambdaMaxCm: 1e-1, // 1 mm`. Line 44 is `examples: "Microwave ovens, CMB, molecular clouds, radar"`. Line 34 does list "the cosmic microwave background" in the Radio examples. `radio` at logic.ts:29-30 is `1e-1` to `1e6` cm, so the demo has effectively named the submillimetre band "Microwave" and swallowed the real microwave band into Radio.

2. My own numbers (`node -e`, c = 2.99792458e10 cm/s, Wien b = 0.289777 cm K), not the finder's:
- Microwave band edges: 1e-2 cm = 2.998 THz; 1e-1 cm = 299.79 GHz. So the band is 300 GHz to 3.0 THz = submillimetre/terahertz, not microwave (conventionally 1 mm to 1 m, 300 MHz to 300 GHz).
- Oven, 2.45 GHz: lambda = 12.2364 cm.
- X-band radar, 10 GHz: lambda = 2.9979 cm.
- CO(1-0), 115.271 GHz: lambda = 0.26008 cm = 2.6008 mm.
- CMB, T = 2.72548 K: per-wavelength peak lambda = b/T = 0.10632 cm = 1.0632 mm; per-frequency peak nu = 160.229 GHz -> lambda = 0.18710 cm = 1.871 mm. Either convention exceeds 1e-1 cm.
- `bandCenterCm("microwave")` = sqrt(1e-2 x 1e-1) = 3.1623e-2 cm = 316.2 um.
I re-implemented `bandFromWavelengthCm` from logic.ts:182-199 in plain JS and ran it: 12.2364 -> radio, 2.9979 -> radio, 0.26008 -> radio, 0.106319 -> radio. All four of the Microwave card's own examples classify as Radio.

3. Reachable by a student. index.html:36 exposes `<button class="cp-chip band" data-band="microwave">Microwave</button>`. main.ts:365 reads `data-band`, main.ts:359 calls `setWavelengthCm(bandCenterCm(key))` -> marker lands at 316 um. main.ts:222-231 writes `band.name` to `bandBadge`/`bandName`, `band.examples` to `bandExamples`, and `formatWavelength(band.lambdaMinCm/MaxCm)` as the printed range, so the card literally reads "Microwave, 100 um to 1 mm, Microwave ovens, CMB, molecular clouds, radar". main.ts:345 then recomputes `state.band = bandFromWavelengthCm(lambdaCm)` on every slider move, so dragging toward 12 cm flips the badge to Radio. Not already fixed and not handled elsewhere. `git log -3 -- .../em-spectrum/logic.ts` ends at 8fcedd6 "Fix the seasons terminator and the em-spectrum gradient"; `git status --porcelain` on the demo and on packages/data-spectra is empty, so the committed state is the live state. Tests encode the defect, exactly as the project memory warns. logic.test.ts:459-462 only asserts internal contiguity (`radio.min == microwave.max`), which stays green under any wrong placement. logic.test.ts:363-364 is `it("returns microwave for 3 mm", () => expect(bandFromWavelengthCm(0.03)).toBe("microwave"))` — 0.03 cm is 0.3 mm, not 3 mm, so the test name states the author's correct intent (3 mm should be microwave) while the assertion pins the 10x-wrong value that satisfies the defective band. The demo's first stated learning goal (apps/site/src/content/demos/em-spectrum.md:14, "Order EM bands by wavelength and frequency") is the exact thing it gets wrong, by two to three decades, in reader-visible copy a student has no way to check. findings.title: Simpson on the sqrt-singular Fermi integrand makes P_deg,e 24.8% high at eos-lab's default solar-core state, and up to 2.5x high along the weak-degeneracy edge
findings.evidence: `intervals: 192` (lines 415 and 469) applies Simpson's rule to `rootY * occ` = y^{1/2} f(y-eta) over [0, yMax]. The sqrt endpoint singularity at y=0 destroys Simpson's 4th order. I reimplemented the shipped algorithm exactly in plain JS (linspace + the same h/3 weights + the same bisection) and reproduced the shipped value to 6 significant figures, then refined the interval count. At the Solar-core preset (T = 1.57e7 K, rho = 150 g cm^-3, X=0.34/Y=0.64/Z=0.02): P_e,FD = 1.36998e17 (N=192), 1.36238e17 (384), 1.35981e17 (768), 1.35892e17 (1536), 1.35845e17 (49152) dyne cm^-2 -- the error halves on each doubling, i.e. FIRST order, not fourth. n_e k_B T = 1.311897e17 dyne cm^-2, so the displayed excess is 5.808087e15 (shipped) vs 4.654806e15 (converged) dyne cm^-2: +24.8%. The 0.85% error in P_e,FD is amplified ~29x by subtracting a quantity 96% as large. P_tot is also 0.49% high (2.35054e17 vs 2.33894e17) and beta reads 97.46% instead of 97.95%.
findings.scenario: A student opens /play/eos-lab/ -- the initial state IS solar-core (main.ts:387) -- and reads the P_deg,e card as 5.808e15 dyne cm^-2. The correct value is 4.655e15. The first significant digit is wrong. The same number flows into the P_deg,e/P_tot readout, the copy-results export, and every station-mode table row a student hands in. The weakly-degenerate part of the P_deg curve on the chart is systematically too high, shifting where a student reads the gas/degeneracy crossover.
findings.fix:
Apply the finding's substitution, in both non-relativistic call sites, with my converged reference values rather than its.

1. packages/physics/src/stellarEosModel.ts, `electronPressureFiniteTNonRelDynePerCm2`: change the integration variable to s = sqrt(y) in BOTH `simpsonIntegratePair` calls — the residual at :412-424 and the final pressure integral at :468-478. Integrate over s in [0, sqrt(yMax)] with `numberIntegrand: 2*s*s*occ` and `pressureIntegrand: 2*Math.pow(s,4)*occ`, where `occ = fermiOccupation(s*s - eta)`. Keep yMax = max(40, eta+40) and keep `intervals: 192` — I measured <0.01% error on the excess at N=192 over the entire branch window (chi 5 down to 1.2e-3, eta -2.7 to +833), so no cost increase is needed. Leave the relativistic branch (:521, :564) alone: its q = sinh u substitution already makes the integrand analytic at the origin, and I confirmed no sqrt singularity there.

2. packages/physics/src/stellarEosModel.test.ts: re-derive the two pinned solar-core references from the substituted integral, not from the previous output. electronDegeneracyPressureDynePerCm2 (:509) -> 4.6545423e15 dyne cm^-2 and totalPressureDynePerCm2 (:511) -> 2.3390031e17 dyne cm^-2 (my converged values; the finding's 4.654806e15 / 2.338935e17 still carry its own 0.006% / 0.003% residual). The gas (:507) and radiation (:508) references are closed-form and unaffected; chiDegeneracy and fermiRelativityX are unaffected. Tighten the two tolerances from 5e-4 to ~1e-6 once the quadrature is converged — the loose 5e-4 is what let the old value pass as "verified".

3. Add two tests, not one. (a) The convergence test the finding proposes: doubling `intervals` changes P_deg,e by <0.1% at the solar-core state. (b) A branch-continuity test the finding misses: the shipped P_deg,e curve jumps by a factor ~2.5 across the chi=8 boundary where line 606-612 hands over to `classical-limit` (excess 0 by construction). Assert that P_deg,e is continuous to within a few percent across chi = 8 and across x_F = 0.3, evaluated just either side — otherwise the chart keeps a visible step that a student reads as physics.

4. After the fix, the eos-lab `P_deg,e` card, the copy-results export, the station table and both chart curves all move; the solar-core card goes from 5.808e15 to 4.655e15 dyne cm^-2 and beta from 97.46% to 97.95%. Any instructor key or screenshot carrying the old numbers needs regenerating, and this should land before eos-lab is moved off `readiness: experimental` / `unlisted: true`.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED by independent recomputation with a different method than the finder used.

1. Code exists as quoted. `packages/physics/src/stellarEosModel.ts:415` and `:469` both pass `intervals: 192` to `simpsonIntegratePair` over `[0, yMax]` with integrands `rootY*occ` = y^(1/2)f(y-eta) and `y*rootY*occ` = y^(3/2)f(y-eta) (lines 416-423, 470-477). `simpsonIntegratePair` (line 323) builds a uniform `linspace` grid and calls `integrateSimpsonSamples` (packages/math/src/math.ts:65), which applies the plain h/3 · [1,4,2,...,4,1] rule — so the y^(1/2) endpoint singularity at y=0 is hit directly. The prefactors are correct physics: I re-derived prefactorN = 4*pi*(2 m_e k_B T)^(3/2)/h^3 and prefactorP = 4*pi*(2 m_e k_B T)^(5/2)/(3 h^3 m_e) from n = (8pi/h^3)∫p^2 f dp and P = (8pi/3h^3 m)∫p^4 f dp with g=2; both match lines 403-407. The defect is purely quadrature.

2. Independent recomputation (I did NOT reuse the finder's arithmetic). Solar-core state: T = 1.57e7 K, rho = 150 g cm^-3, X/Y/Z = 0.34/0.64/0.02 -> mu_e = 1.4925373134, n_e = 6.0522514659e25 cm^-3, n_e k_B T = 1.3118974847e17 dyne cm^-2. I computed the FD integrals two ways:
  - Gauss-Legendre after the substitution y = s^2 (my own GL nodes via Newton on P_n), s in [0, sqrt(120)]: eta = -1.531165547790, P_e,FD = 1.3584429079e17 dyne cm^-2 — identical to 11 digits at nGL = 40, 80, 160, 320.
  - Reimplementation of the shipped scheme (linspace + h/3 Simpson in y + the same bracket/bisection): N=192 -> 1.36997836e17; 384 -> 1.36237921e17; 768 -> 1.35981241e17; 1536 -> 1.35892343e17; 49152 -> 1.35844555e17 dyne cm^-2, converging to my GL value.
  Excess P_deg,e = P_e,FD - n_e k_B T: shipped 5.80808708e15 vs converged 4.6545423e15 dyne cm^-2 = +24.78%. P_tot: 2.3505386e17 (shipped) vs 2.3390031e17 (converged) = +0.49%. beta = P_gas/P_tot: 97.464% vs 97.945%. Every number the finding claimed reproduces.

3. Reachable and live. chi = T/T_F = 2.408 (not <=1e-3, not >=8) and x_F = 0.0469 < 0.3, so `electronPressureFiniteTDynePerCm2` (line 583) takes the `nonrel-fd` branch at line 617. The demo's initial state is `solar-core` (apps/demos/src/demos/eos-lab/main.ts:387-390, applied again at :1411). The value reaches the P_deg card (main.ts:793), the copy-results export (main.ts:675, 678-679, 1221, 1247), the station table (main.ts:1247), and both chart curves (logic.ts:290, 666). /play/eos-lab/ is built and deployed (apps/site/public/play/eos-lab exists); `unlisted: true` only removes it from the catalogue listing — catalog.ts:23 states play/exhibit/station pages are kept so shared links survive.

4. Not already fixed or guarded. `git log -3` on the file: 0f75490 (Biome lint), 19baaf9, 6f977e0 — none touches the quadrature. `grep intervals:` shows only 192/192/224/224, unchanged.

5. The defect is BROADER than claimed, not milder. Simpson in y errs as ~h^(3/2) via eta (error ratio 2.85 per doubling, i.e. order ~1.5 — the finding's "halves on each doubling, FIRST order" is slightly wrong, which does not change anything). Because the excess shrinks toward the weak-degeneracy edge while the absolute quadrature error does not, the relative error grows: at T=1e7 K, chi=6 -> +102%, chi=7 -> +129%, chi=7.9 -> +156%. A grid sweep at X=0.7 gives +157% (logT=5, rho=1e-2 and logT=7, rho=10), +88% (logT=7.5, rho=100), +48% (logT=8, rho=1e3). So the P_deg,e curve is up to 2.5x too high along the whole weakly-degenerate side, and it jumps discontinuously by ~2.5x at the chi=8 switch to `classical-limit` (line 606-612), where the excess is zero by construction. The brown-dwarf preset is only +0.3% (strongly degenerate); the other four presets route to `classical-limit` or `rel-fd` and are unaffected.

6. The existing test pins the defect. stellarEosModel.test.ts:509 asserts electronDegeneracyPressureDynePerCm2 ≈ 5.808123130210272e15 at tol 5e-4; my reproduction of the shipped N=192 path gives 5.80808708e15, a 6e-6 relative match. The reference was taken from the output, not derived — the memory lesson "tests encode defects" applies literally here.

7. Severity corrected P0 -> P1. The number is genuinely wrong in the default view of a live page, which is P0-grade. But eos-lab is honestly quarantined: apps/site/src/content/demos/eos-lab.md has `status: draft`, `readiness: experimental`, `unlisted: true`, and a public unlistedReason saying the EOS is incomplete and "Withheld from the catalogue until the EOS is complete and independently checked." A student browsing the site cannot land on it; only a direct/shared link reaches it, and the exhibit page carries the on-hold banner (exhibits/[slug].astro:59-63). The readiness claims do not outrun the evidence, so this is not also a readiness-honesty finding. It becomes P0 the instant eos-lab is promoted, and it must block that promotion.

8. The proposed fix is correct — I verified it. With y = s^2 (number integrand 2 s^2 f(s^2-eta), pressure 2 s^4 f(s^2-eta), s in [0, sqrt(yMax)]), Simpson gives the converged P_e,FD = 1.3584429079e17 to 11 digits at N = 48, 96, 192, 384 and 3072. Across the whole nonrel-fd window (chi from 5 down to 1.2e-3, eta from -2.7 to +833) the substituted Simpson at N=192 errs by <0.01% on the excess, including the strongly degenerate corner where I expected the Fermi edge to under-resolve. The finding's two reference values are slightly unconverged, though (they are its N=49152 Simpson-in-y outputs): use 4.6545423e15 and 2.3390031e17 dyne cm^-2, not 4.654806e15 and 2.338935e17 (0.006% and 0.003% off).

findings.title: Regime map's hardcoded "GAS" label is drawn on degeneracy-dominated cells, ~5 dex above the gas region (P_deg/P_gas = 1347 there)
findings.evidence: `ctx.fillText("GAS", logTToX(5.5, pa, cfg), logRhoToY(6, pa, cfg));` -- a hardcoded (log T = 5.5, log rho = 6) regardless of composition. I evaluated the model's own channels there with the default composition (X=0.34, Y=0.64, Z=0.02, mu_e = 1.4925): n_e = 4.035e29 cm^-3, x_F = 0.883, T/T_F = 1.60e-4 (zero-T branch), P_gas = 3.076e19, P_rad = 2.52e7, P_deg,e = 4.144e22 dyne cm^-2. Degeneracy wins by a factor of 1347, so classifyDominantPressure returns "degeneracy" and drawExactGrid fills that cell violet -- with the word GAS printed on top of it. Same verdict for an H-rich composition (X=0.74: P_deg/P_gas = 1413). Scanning the plane at 0.25-dex resolution, the 489 gas-dominated cells have centroid (log T = 5.23, log rho = -2.95). The RAD label at (8, -6) and the DEG label at (4.5, 4) do land in their own regions.
findings.scenario: A student opens the Regime Map panel, reads the violet region labelled "GAS", and concludes that rho = 10^6 g cm^-3 at T = 3x10^5 K is gas-pressure supported -- i.e. that a white-dwarf-density plasma is thermally supported. The colour fill, the dashed analytical gas/degeneracy boundary and the legend all say degeneracy; only the printed word says gas, and the word is what a student reads first.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED. I could not refute it; I reproduced it twice, independently of the finder's arithmetic.

1. Code exists as quoted. `/Users/anna/Teaching/cosmic-playground/apps/demos/src/demos/eos-lab/regimeMap.ts:256` is verbatim `ctx.fillText("GAS", logTToX(5.5, pa, cfg), logRhoToY(6, pa, cfg));`, inside `drawAnalyticalOverlay` (lines 219-263), alongside `RAD` at (8, -6) on :259 and `DEG` at (4.5, 4) on :262. All three anchors are literals; the function already receives `mu` and `muE` but uses neither for label placement.

2. Independent recomputation (my own plain-JS CGS implementation of rho k T/(mu m_u), a T^4/3, and the zero-T relativistic electron pressure (m_e^4 c^5 / 24 pi^2 hbar^3)[x(2x^2-3)sqrt(1+x^2) + 3 asinh x], then the model's own `max(0, P_e - n_e k T)` excess and `classifyDominantPressure`'s `second/top >= 0.8 -> mixed` rule). At (log T = 5.5, log rho = 6) with the demo's default composition (PRESETS "solar-core", main.ts:390 -> main.ts:203, X=0.34 Y=0.64 Z=0.02): mu = 0.854701, mu_e = 1.492537, n_e = 4.0348e29 cm^-3, x_F = 0.88277, T_F = 1.9800e9 K, T/T_F = 1.597e-4 (so the zero-T branch at stellarEosModel.ts:602 fires). P_gas = 3.0762e19, P_rad = 2.5219e7, P_deg = 4.1440e22 dyne cm^-2. P_deg/P_gas = 1347.1; second/top = 7.42e-4, so `classifyDominantPressure` returns "degeneracy" and that cell is painted violet (#a78bfa) while the word GAS is drawn on it in green (#34d399). Every digit the finder quoted reproduces.

3. Second, independent route. The dashed analytical NR gas=deg boundary at log T = 5.5 is log rho = 1.165 (recomputed from `gasDegBoundaryLogRho`'s own closed form with K_NR = (3 pi^2)^(2/3) hbar^2 / (5 m_e)). The gas band at that temperature is log rho in [-6.086, +1.165], midpoint -2.46. So the label sits 4.84 dex above the top of the gas region and ~8.5 dex from its centre. The other two labels do land correctly: RAD (8, -6) has P_rad = 2.52e17 vs P_gas = 9.73e9 (radiation by 2.6e7); DEG (4.5, 4) has P_deg/P_gas = 766.

4. Reachable, unguarded, and live by default. The regime map is in the default tab (index.html:306-310, `tab-explore` has `aria-selected="true"`, `#panel-explore` is not `hidden`), the canvas is `#regimeMapCanvas` at index.html:289. main.ts:766 calls `renderRegimeMap` with no config, so `DEFAULT_CONFIG.showAnalyticalOverlay = true` (regimeMap.ts:67) and regimeMap.ts:513-516 draws the overlay unconditionally. The labels are not clipped (logRhoToY(6) = 20% down the plot area, logTToX(5.5) = 41.7% across). Both grid paths agree: the main-thread `evaluateRegimeGrid` (logic.ts:457) and `regimeWorker.ts` both call the same `StellarEosModel.evaluateStateCgs`, so the violet fill under the label is identical either way. The tour callout at main.ts:1487 points a first-time reader straight at this canvas: "This map shows which pressure dominates at every (T, rho) combination."

5. Not already fixed. `git log -5 -- .../regimeMap.ts` ends at 58b55e6 (worker move); the three literals predate it and survive. `git status --porcelain apps/demos/src/demos/eos-lab/` is clean. No guard anywhere: nothing reads the grid when placing labels. No test pins placement either — design-contracts.test.ts:87-90 only greps regimeMap.ts for the strings "renderRegimeMap", "invalidateRegimeGrid", "evaluateRegimeGrid", and logic.test.ts touches only `regimeMapCoordinates`. So this would not have been caught.

Two corrections to the finding's framing, neither refuting it:
(a) "nine decades off" measures the distance to the gas region's *centroid*. The distance to the nearest gas-dominated density at the label's own temperature is 4.84 dex. Both are large; the title should say so precisely.
(b) The finder calls the one-line move a stopgap that "will drift again when composition changes". It does not. I evaluated (5.2, -3.0) at the four extreme compositions reachable from the UI (X=0.34, X=0.74, pure H X=1, and the white-dwarf preset X=0/Y=0.98) and it classifies as "gas" in all four, because mu and mu_e vary by less than a factor of 2 (shifting the boundaries ~0.3 dex) while the gas band is ~7 dex wide. Conversely the current GAS anchor is wrong for all four compositions I tested, including X=0/Y=0.98, so this is not a default-only accident.

Adjacent defect found while tracing, not part of this finding: `drawExactGrid` (regimeMap.ts:190-213) has a half-cell offset. `evaluateRegimeGrid` samples at logT = logTMin + i*(6/99) and logRho = logRhoMin + j*(20/79), but the fill places cell i,j at pa.x + i*(pa.w/100), i.e. on a 6/100 and 20/80 pitch, so painted cells are displaced up to ~0.06 dex in T and ~0.25 dex in rho from the state they represent, and the top row/right column are drawn outside their own data. Worth a separate P2.

Severity upheld at P0 under this project's rubric ("wrong drawing a student would believe"): the word is the most salient element in the panel, it names the wrong physical regime, it is on screen on first load, and it asserts that a white-dwarf-density plasma (rho = 10^6 g cm^-3 at T = 3.16e5 K, where degeneracy wins by 1347x) is thermally supported — the exact misconception this panel exists to dispel. The mitigating facts (fill colour, legend, dashed boundary, and the `regimeSummary` line at main.ts:786 all say degeneracy; nothing numeric is miscomputed) make it a mild P0, an annotation error rather than a model error, so the fix touches no physics.

findings.title: The "Dark matter inference" card prints the spherical estimator V^2R/G - M_vis(<R), which overstates the demo's own M_dark readout by 1.42e10 Msun in the No-dark-matter preset (readout 0.000) and by 36-48% in Milky-Way-like
findings.evidence: index.html:228 renders `$$M_{\rm dark}(<R)=\frac{V_{\rm obs}^2R}{G}-M_{\rm vis}(<R)$$` to the student. But the demo's M_dark readout is the NFW halo enclosed mass (galaxyRotationModel.ts:551 `mDark10: masses.dark`), and V^2R/G is not the enclosed mass of a disk. I recomputed both quantities from an independent transcription of the model. no-dark-matter preset (haloMass10 = 0): R = 3 kpc -> readout M_dark = 0.000, displayed equation = 0.179; R = 7 kpc -> 0.000 vs 1.287; R = 10 kpc -> 0.000 vs 1.421 (units 1e10 Msun). milky-way-like: R = 5 kpc -> readout 1.495 vs equation 2.207 (+47.6%); R = 8 kpc -> 3.307 vs 4.508 (+36.3%); R = 7 kpc -> 2.654 vs 3.761 (+41.7%). My +47.6% and +36.3% reproduce prior finding GR-2 (docs/reviews/galaxy-rotation.md:23, logged 2026-09-03, status 'open') to the decimal.
findings.scenario: A student follows play_steps[0] ("Start with `No dark matter`"), reads V_total = 154 km/s at R = 10 kpc off the plot, applies the equation printed on the Understand tab, gets M_dark = 1.4e10 Msun, and concludes that even the no-dark-matter galaxy needs dark matter — in a preset built to have none. The readout one panel away says 0.000. The error runs in the direction that overstates the evidence for dark matter, which is the demo's own headline claim.
findings.fix:
The proposed fix (label the card "spherical estimate" plus a caveat line) would stop the card being wrong, but it settles for a caveat where the demo already has the exact relation. Make it exact instead, in three parts:

(a) apps/demos/src/demos/galaxy-rotation/index.html:228 — replace the card with the relation the readout actually implements, which I verified is an exact identity for mDark10 in all four presets:
$$M_{\rm dark}(<R)=\frac{\left(V_{\rm total}^2-V_{\rm vis}^2\right)R}{G}$$
plus one line: both velocities are read off the two plotted curves, and this is exact because the halo is spherical. The card then reproduces the readout to machine precision, including 0.000 for No-dark-matter, and the Understand tab stops contradicting index.html:373.

(b) Keep the single-velocity estimator as its own explicitly-labeled card, because the disk-vs-sphere gap is a genuinely good lesson — the finder's instinct here is right. Title it "Spherical estimate from one velocity", print $M_{\rm sph}(<R)=V^2R/G$, and quote the measured gap: at R = 10 kpc in No-dark-matter, M_sph = 6.75 vs M(<R) = 5.33 (1e10 Msun), +26.7%, because a disk's in-plane force exceeds GM(<R)/R^2. Implement it with the already-existing GalaxyRotationModel.massFromVelocity10 (galaxyRotationModel.ts:516), which is currently dead outside the test file — that satisfies the no-inline-equations invariant and removes the dead-code smell in one move. If you add it as a readout, put it in the "Inputs and mass budget" accordion rather than the primary group, which already holds four values.

(c) Replace the vacuous test at packages/physics/src/galaxyRotationModel.test.ts:294. Assert on milky-way-like and massive-spiral (where the halo is non-zero, so the assertion can actually fail) that (vTotal^2 - vVisible^2)*R/G equals mDark10 to within 1e-9, and add one test pinning massFromVelocity10({velocityKmS: vVisible, radiusKpc}) - mVisible10 > 0 with the magnitude the new card quotes at R = 10 kpc. Do not re-use the no-dark-matter preset for the first assertion: it is identically zero by construction there.

Also update the GR-2 row at docs/reviews/galaxy-rotation.md:23 — it is marked "same root cause as GR-1", and GR-1 is fixed, so GR-2 is one bookkeeping pass away from being closed without anyone changing line 228.

findings.scenario: A student at guided step 2 ('local-shell') reads the prompt 'Which side has to push harder for the shell to stay balanced?' and clicks Balanced -> Under-supported -> Over-supported. findings.fix:
Two changes in `renderHeroSvg`, both in apps/demos/src/demos/hydrostatic-equilibrium-explorer/main.ts.

(a) main.ts:430 — separate the mode-independent pedagogical exaggeration from the mode-dependent asymmetry, keeping the saturating tanh only for the baseline. Read the support factor in the function (`const supportFactor = supportFactorForMode(state.supportMode);`, already exported from logic.ts) and replace line 430 with:

    const balancedContrast = pressureContrast / supportFactor;           // mode-independent
    const asymmetryBase = 18 * Math.tanh(balancedContrast * 110);        // the deliberate exaggeration
    const supportGain = Math.max(0.15, 1 + 2.2 * (supportFactor - 1));   // never lets asymmetry invert

(b) main.ts:435-440 — make the force arrows share a mode-independent scale so gravity stops changing when only the support factor does: `const forceReference = Math.max(Math.abs(patch.gravitationalForceDyne), 1);`. Then add a design-contract assertion that renders the hero at one shell radius for all three support modes and requires the inner-minus-outer arrow asymmetry to be strictly increasing in supportFactor and strictly positive in each mode — the existing tests assert nothing about these arrows, which is why the saturation shipped.

findings.title: Newton-mode v and F arrows are drawn at a fixed 60 px and 40 px, so Kepler 2 and the inverse-square law are drawn as constant (vScale divides by the instantaneous speed, not the per-orbit maximum its own name claims)
findings.evidence: main.ts:393-394: `const maxSpeed = stateAtM.speedAuPerYr; const vScale = maxSpeed > 0 ? 60 / maxSpeed : 0;` then x2 = pos.x + vx*vScale, y2 = pos.y - vy*vScale (lines 399-400). Drawn length = sqrt((vx*vScale)^2+(vy*vScale)^2) = |v| * 60/|v| = 60 px for every state. main.ts:403: `const fLen = 40;` with the endpoint from a pure direction angle (line 402), so the force arrow is also exactly 40 px regardless of r. I recomputed the two states the arrows are meant to contrast, Halley (a=17.8, e=0.967): perihelion r=0.587 AU, v=10.223 AU/yr, a_grav=114.5 AU/yr^2; aphelion r=35.01 AU, v=0.1715 AU/yr, a_grav=0.0322 AU/yr^2. The speed ratio is 59.6x and the force ratio is 3554x; both arrows are drawn at the same length at both ends.
findings.scenario: Student picks Newton mode, the Halley preset, ticks Vectors, and scrubs from perihelion to aphelion. The speed readout drops from 48.5 km/s to 0.81 km/s but the 'v' arrow never changes length, and the 'F' arrow never changes length either. The intended reading of the figure is 'longer arrow = faster / stronger pull'; the student concludes speed and gravitational force are constant around the orbit, which is the exact misconception the exhibit's `misconceptions` field says the demo exists to break.
findings.fix:
Scale both arrows against a per-orbit reference taken at perihelion, but map the force arrow nonlinearly and label the convention — do not rely on a minimum-length clamp, which on the Halley preset pins the v arrow for 71% and the F arrow for 99% of the period.

In a new pure function in apps/demos/src/demos/keplers-laws/logic.ts (so it is unit-testable, per the project's "no inline logic in main.ts" habit):

  vectorLengthsPx({ speedAuPerYr, accelAuPerYr2, aAu, e, muAu3Yr2 }) with
    rPeri = aAu * (1 - e)
    vPeri = sqrt(mu * (2/rPeri - 1/aAu))        // vis-viva, reuse TwoBodyAnalytic.visVivaSpeedAuPerYr
    aGravPeri = mu / rPeri^2
    vPx = 60 * (speedAuPerYr / vPeri)                      // linear: speed spans only ~60x, honest
    fPx = 40 * sqrt(accelAuPerYr2 / aGravPeri)             // sqrt: 1/r^2 becomes 1/r in pixels

The sqrt map turns the inverse-square into an inverse-first-power in drawn length, so Halley's aphelion force arrow is 40*sqrt(1/3553) = 0.67 px rather than 0.011 px — still small, and correctly small, because the pull really is 3,553x weaker. Keep a floor of 2 px (not 6) purely so the arrowhead marker still renders, and set the arrow's stroke-width from the same ratio so a short arrow also reads as thin rather than as a stub.

Then, because the drawn force length is no longer proportional to the force, the convention has to be stated or it becomes a new misleading drawing:
  - put it in the SVG <title>/aria description and in the overlay's label copy, authored as KaTeX per CLAUDE.md: "arrow lengths are relative to perihelion; $|v|$ is drawn to scale, $|F|$ is drawn as $\sqrt{F/F_{\rm peri}}$ so the full range fits"
  - the numeric readouts (velocity km/s, acceleration mm/s^2, already present at main.ts:508,535) stay the quantitative channel.

Also fix the two adjacent defects in the same function while it is open: move #velocityLabel and #forceLabel to the arrow tips each frame (they are currently never repositioned, so "v" and "F" sit at their authored coordinates far from the arrows), and rename `maxSpeed` out of existence since that name is what produced the bug.

Tests to add in logic.test.ts, asserting on the returned numbers (not on element presence): at e=0.967 the perihelion/aphelion vPx ratio equals the vis-viva speed ratio to within 1e-9; fPx(peri)/fPx(aph) equals sqrt(3552.9) to within 1e-9; and a regression guard that vPx is NOT equal at perihelion and aphelion — the assertion that would have caught today's bug.
