7. The proposed fix is directionally right but its clamp swallows the effect on the very preset the finding is about. With vRef = v(perihelion) and a 6 px floor, I computed on Halley: the aphelion velocity arrow would be 1.007 px and the force arrow 0.0113 px, both under the floor — the v arrow sits pinned at 6 px for 71.28% of the orbital period and the F arrow for 99.47% (uniform sampling in mean anomaly, which is uniform in time, N = 200,000). So the student would see a constant floor-length arrow for most of the orbit with a spike only near perihelion: better than today, but still reads as "constant", and for the force it is effectively no change. A linear scale cannot show 3.5 decades of inverse-square in 40 px.

findings.title: Orbit view auto-normalizes to a fixed 150 px semi-major axis with no scale bar, so Kepler 3's size change has no visual channel above 1 AU and the zoom rule silently inverts below it
findings.evidence: main.ts:182 `const scale = SVG_SCALE / Math.max(state.aAu, 1);` with SVG_SCALE = 150 (line 19); updateOrbitPath uses `rx = state.aAu * scale` (line 263). So rx = a * 150/max(a,1) = 150 px for every a >= 1. I computed rx for each preset: a=0.387 -> 58.05 px, a=0.723 -> 108.45 px, a=1 -> 150.00 px, a=1.524 -> 150.00 px, a=5.203 -> 150.00 px, a=17.8 -> 150.00 px, a=39.48 -> 150.00 px. Nothing in the SVG reports the scale: there is no scale bar, no axis, no AU ruler (index.html:31-161 has no such element), and the only distance cue is the r readout text.
findings.scenario: Student follows play_steps 3 in keplers-laws.md ('Compare two semi-major axes a (same M) and observe how the period P changes') by clicking Earth then Pluto. Pluto's orbit is 39.5x larger, but the drawing is pixel-identical in size; only the dashed ellipse's eccentricity and the numbers change. The student reads the figure as 'the orbit is the same, only the clock changed' and cannot connect orbit size to period — and below 1 AU the behaviour silently inverts (Mercury draws smaller), so the zoom rule is not even consistent.
findings.fix:
1. Declare the scale. Add a scale-bar group to the SVG (index.html, near distanceText) whose length and label are recomputed each frame from `scale`: pick the largest step from {0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20} AU whose pixel length falls in [60, 150] px and label it with KaTeX via `renderMath()` from `@cosmic/runtime` (`$1\ \mathrm{AU}$`), per the repo's KaTeX-only rule — not a Unicode or bare-ASCII label in reader-visible text. This supplies the information that is actually missing.

2. Give Kepler 3 a visual channel without a fixed linear scale. Keep the auto-fit, and on each a/e change draw a ghost ellipse of the PREVIOUS a and e at the CURRENT scale. Earth -> Jupiter then shows the Earth ghost at 1/5.2 the new ellipse (rx 28.8 px vs 150 px), which is exactly the comparison play_steps 3 asks for, and it stays legible across the whole 0.3-40 AU range. The state already carries `periodReferenceYr` and `pendingPeriodComparison` for the delta-P hint (main.ts:575-582), so hang the ghost on that same transition and the figure and the `$\Delta P$: $\times N$` hint tell one story.

3. Do NOT fix the scale at 150/40 px/AU. Computed above: Mercury through Jupiter (1.45-19.51 px) all land inside the r=20 px star glyph (index.html:97), which makes the inner solar system unreadable — strictly worse than today.

4. Remove the unexplained floor and the duplication. `Math.max(state.aAu, 1)` makes the view fit-to-a above 1 AU and fixed at 150 px/AU below it, so the zoom rule changes character at a=1 for no stated reason. Either use `SVG_SCALE / state.aAu` (pure fit, consistent everywhere) or keep the floor and say why in a comment. Extract it once into logic.ts as `pxPerAu(aAu)` — note the finding's `auPerPixel` name is inverted; `scale` is px per AU — and have all four call sites (main.ts:182, 262, 325, 342) use it.

5. Test the extracted function, not a tautology. Assert `pxPerAu` is strictly decreasing in a across 0.3-40 (which fails today, since it is flat at 150 below 1 AU), and that the scale-bar step picker returns a bar length within [60, 150] px at a = 0.3, 1, 5.203 and 39.48.
findings.note:
The geometric claim reproduces exactly; the severity and one evidence line do not.

CODE EXISTS AS QUOTED. `apps/demos/src/demos/keplers-laws/main.ts:19` `const SVG_SCALE = 150;`; `:182` `const scale = SVG_SCALE / Math.max(state.aAu, 1);` (in `orbitalToSvg`); `:262-265` the same expression in `updateOrbitPath`, with `rx = state.aAu * scale`, `ry = state.aAu * Math.sqrt(1 - state.e*state.e) * scale`, `c = state.aAu * state.e * scale`. Same expression repeated at `:325` (`updateFociMarkers`) and `:342` (`updateApsidesMarkers`) — four copies, which is the DRY half of the finding and is real.

MY OWN RECOMPUTATION (node, not the finder's arithmetic). rx = a * 150/max(a,1): a=0.3 -> 45.00 px; a=0.387 -> 58.05 px; a=0.723 -> 108.45 px; a=1.0 -> 150.00 px; a=1.524 -> 150.00 px; a=2 -> 150.00 px; a=5.203 -> 150.00 px; a=9.54 -> 150.00 px; a=17.8 -> 150.00 px; a=39.48 -> 150.00 px; a=40 -> 150.00 px. And the whole ellipse is pixel-identical, not just rx: at e=0.2, a=1 / 5.203 / 39.48 all give ry=146.97 px and c=30.00 px. px-per-AU falls from 150.0000 at a=1 to 3.7994 at a=39.48. Confirmed: for every a >= 1 AU the orbit drawing is identical to the pixel, and below 1 AU it shrinks linearly instead, so the zoom rule changes character at a=1.

NO SCALE CUE IN THE FIGURE. I read the full SVG (index.html:31-161): defs, orbitPath, equalAreasGroup, fociGroup, apsidesGroup, star, distanceLine, velocity/force vectors, planetGroup, distanceText. No scale bar, no axis, no AU ruler; `grep -rn 'scale-bar|scaleBar|scale bar|px per AU|pxPerAu|ruler'` over the demo directory returns nothing (exit 1).

REACHABLE AND LIVE. The `a` slider is 0.3-40 AU on a log scale (index.html:233-235) and presets expose 0.387 to 39.48 (index.html:325-338). No clamp or guard. The SVG is the visible layer: `.orbit-canvas` is `opacity: 0; pointer-events: none` (style.css:45-52) and `drawOrbitCanvas` only fills one planet dot (main.ts:318-321), so main.ts:182/263 is the path a student actually sees. Not already fixed: `git log -3` on main.ts is 57f01c0 (equal-areas wedge size), a2d6d31 ([hidden] vs author display), 0f75490 (Biome) — nothing touching scale.

WHERE THE FINDING IS WRONG. (1) "the only distance cue is the r readout text" is false. `overlays.apsides` defaults to `true` (main.ts:136-141), and `updateApsidesMarkers` writes `Perihelion (X AU)` and `Aphelion (X AU)` into the figure each frame (main.ts:413, 424), alongside the always-visible `r = X AU` (main.ts:378) and the `a` display. On Earth -> Pluto those in-figure labels change 0.98/1.02 AU -> 29.6/49.3 AU under the markers. So the drawing is accompanied by its own correct, contradicting numbers. (2) Severity P0 is too harsh. Nothing is numerically or geometrically wrong — shape, focus offset, eccentricity and every label are correct at every a; the view is normalized, and the defect is that the normalization is undeclared and discontinuous, so Kepler 3's size->period comparison has no visual channel. That is a misleading-presentation / missing-affordance defect, i.e. P1 under this audit's own rubric, not a wrong number or wrong drawing. The demo also already carries `status: draft`, `readiness: experimental`, `readinessReason: "...parity and launch-gate signoff are still pending."` (apps/site/src/content/demos/keplers-laws.md:3, 11-12), so there is no readiness-honesty aggravation to push it back to P0.

THE PROPOSED FIX IS PARTLY UNSAFE. "hold the scale fixed at a reference a (e.g. 150/40 px per AU)" = 3.75 px/AU. I computed the drawn rx at that scale against the star glyph, which is `r="20"` px (index.html:97): Mercury 1.45 px, Venus 2.71 px, Earth 3.75 px, Mars 5.71 px, Jupiter 19.51 px — all inside or at the edge of the star circle (plus its `--cp-glow-sun` drop-shadow); only Pluto (148.05 px) is legible. One linear scale cannot span the slider's 133:1 range in a 600x400 viewBox. The suggested unit test is also vacuous: "two different a at a fixed scale give different rx" asserts a1*k != a2*k and would pass against the current buggy code.

findings.title: Both quarter-phase challenges grade on illuminated fraction alone, so each accepts the opposite quarter as correct
findings.evidence: Challenge 3 ("Find the First Quarter Moon position.", line 850) and challenge 4 ("Find the Third Quarter Moon position.", line 870) have byte-identical checks: `const diff = Math.abs(illum - 0.5); if (diff <= 0.03) return { correct: true ... }`. I recomputed: illuminationFractionFromPhaseAngleDeg(90) = 0.5 exactly, so |f - 0.5| = 0 <= 0.03; illuminationFractionFromPhaseAngleDeg(270) = 0.5 + 1.11e-16. The illuminated fraction is identical at both quarters by construction -- f = (1+cos a)/2 is even about a = 180 -- so f alone cannot discriminate them. Nothing in either check reads the angle, the waxing/waning state, or the elongation.
findings.scenario: A student opens Challenge mode, is told "Find the First Quarter Moon position", drags the Moon to the top of the orbital diagram (alpha = 90, Third Quarter, lit on the east/left limb, rises at midnight) and is told "correct, f = 0.500". They have just been confirmed in the single most common lunar-phase misconception, by the demo whose stated job is to teach the distinction, and the hint ('Try alpha near 270') is contradicted by the grader.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED. I could not refute it; everything checked out, and I found an additional, sharper reachability path than the one claimed.

1. Code exists as quoted. /Users/anna/Teaching/cosmic-playground/apps/demos/src/demos/moon-phases/main.ts:850 is `prompt: "Find the First Quarter Moon position."` with hint "Try $\alpha$ near $270^\circ$", and its check at :859 is `const diff = Math.abs(illum - 0.5); if (diff <= 0.03) {correct:true}` / `if (diff <= 0.08) {close:true}`. Line 870 is `prompt: "Find the Third Quarter Moon position."` with hint "Try $\alpha$ near $90^\circ$" and an identical check body at :879 — same thresholds, same messages. Neither check reads angleDeg for anything except the Number.isFinite guard.

2. Independent recomputation (my own node run, not the finder's). packages/physics/src/moonPhasesModel.ts:21-24 is `(1 + Math.cos(radians)) / 2`. I computed:
 - f(90 deg) = 0.500000000000000000, |f - 0.5| = 0.000e+0
 - f(270 deg) = 0.499999999999999889, |f - 0.5| = 1.110e-16
 (The finder wrote 0.5 + 1.11e-16; it is actually 0.5 - 1.11e-16. Immaterial — magnitude is 1.1e-16 either way, 14 orders of magnitude inside the 0.03 band.)
 I also inverted the bands to angle: |f - 0.5| <= 0.03 means |cos alpha| <= 0.06, i.e. alpha within +/-3.44 deg of EITHER 90 or 270; the "close" band |f - 0.5| <= 0.08 is +/-9.21 deg of either (so the finder's "8 deg" for the close band is really 9.21 deg). f = (1 + cos a)/2 satisfies f(180+x) = f(180-x), so f alone provably cannot discriminate the quarters — a mathematical fact, not a tolerance accident.

3. Reachable, and more cheaply than claimed. Traced the control flow end to end: index.html:41 exposes `#btn-challenges`; main.ts:937 toggles `engine.start()`; challengeEngine.ts:302 sets `type = "custom"` because `check` is a function; :418 -> :511-518 routes to the demo's own `check(state)`, with `state` from main.ts:921-924 `getState: () => ({ angleDeg: moonAngleDeg, ... })`; challengeEngine.ts:693 renders the "Check Answer" button; :420-423 shows correct-styled feedback with `result.message` = "$f \approx 0.50$". setAngle (main.ts:353) normalizes into [0,360) with no clamp near the quarters. Keyboard case "7" (main.ts:615) jumps to exactly alpha = 90 and case "3" to exactly 270; logic.ts:16-21 names 90 "Third Quarter" and 270 "First Quarter", matching CLAUDE.md. So on the "Find the First Quarter Moon position" prompt a student can press 7 — or click the on-screen phase button whose data-angle is 90 and which main.ts:475-478 highlights as Third Quarter — then press Check Answer, and be told correct.

4. Not already fixed or guarded. git log -3 on main.ts (4351045, b348a78, 5190637) touches declination, phase-angle guidance and the logic.ts extraction, not the graders. grep for shortestAngleDelta/waxingWaning inside setupChallenges: no hits — the only angle-aware check in the whole challenge array is the shadow challenge (main.ts:905, `normalized < 30 || normalized > 330`). The telling detail: main.ts:471 and :477 already use `Math.abs(shortestAngleDelta(normalized, target))` to highlight the timeline and phase buttons, so the demo distinguishes the two quarters everywhere except in the grader. Both helpers are already imported at main.ts:15-16, so the guard needs no new plumbing.

5. Severity: P0 stands. Nothing displayed is numerically wrong — f = 0.50 is right at both quarters — but an assessment surface returns a false "correct" on an explicitly named wrong position, in the demo whose misconception list and waxing/waning timeline exist to teach that exact distinction. Mitigations I checked and judged insufficient to downgrade: apps/site/src/content/demos/moon-phases.md declares `status: beta` / `readiness: candidate` (so this is not a readiness-honesty violation on top), and the `#phase-name` readout (main.ts:450) does simultaneously display "Third Quarter" at alpha = 90 via the 67.5-112.5 bin in moonPhasesModel.ts:7. A readout contradicting an authoritative "correct" is not a safeguard — the student has no basis to decide which to trust, and CLAUDE.md holds moon-phases up as the golden reference other demos are copied from.

6. The proposed fix works but is incomplete. The angle-distance variant is implementable as written (shortestAngleDelta and normalizeAngle are in scope), though hardcoding 270/90 in the demo duplicates knowledge that packages/physics already owns; I verified the waxing/waning alternative numerically instead: daysSinceNewFromPhaseAngleDeg(270) = (90/360)*29.53 = 7.3825 d < 14.765 -> "Waxing" (correct for First Quarter), and (270/360)*29.53 = 22.148 d -> "Waning" at 90 (correct for Third Quarter). Note the waxing gate alone is NOT sufficient — it would accept alpha = 200 (waxing crescent, f = 0.030) — so it must be ANDed with the existing |f - 0.5| band, which pins alpha to +/-3.44 deg of 270. The gap the finder missed: the prescribed regression test cannot be written where the code lives. logic.test.ts imports only from logic.ts, and main.ts calls requireEl(document.querySelector(...)) at module scope (main.ts:42-52), so importing main.ts in vitest throws before any test runs. The five challenge `check` functions have to be extracted to logic.ts (or a sibling challenges.ts) first, or the fix ships untested — exactly the condition that let this through.

findings.title: Shadow challenge calls any |alpha| < 30 deg "a lunar eclipse alignment" — 32x the physical umbral window (+/-0.95 deg), and outside its own drawn cone past ~18 deg
findings.evidence: `const inShadowZone = normalized < 30 || normalized > 330;` then `message: inShadowZone ? "Yes — that's a lunar eclipse alignment." : ...`. I computed Earth's geometric umbra radius at the Moon's distance: R_umbra = R_earth - (R_sun - R_earth) * d_moon/d_sun = 6378 - (695700-6378) * 3.844e5/1.496e8 = 4607 km, angular radius from Earth atan(4607/3.844e5) = 0.69 deg; the Moon's own angular radius is atan(1737.4/3.844e5) = 0.26 deg, so a partial umbral eclipse needs the Moon within about 0.95 deg of the antisolar point. The demo's window is 30 deg -- 32 times too wide -- and at alpha = 29 the readout simultaneously says "Waning Gibbous, 94% illuminated", which is nobody's eclipse.
findings.scenario: A student completes the shadow challenge at alpha = 25, reads "Yes -- that's a lunar eclipse alignment" next to a 95%-lit gibbous Moon, and concludes lunar eclipses occupy roughly a sixth of every synodic month. That is the opposite of the demo's own misconception target, and it also silently omits the real reason eclipses are rare: the 5.1 deg inclination of the lunar orbit and the node condition, which this 2-D model cannot represent at all.
findings.fix:
Two changes in apps/demos/src/demos/moon-phases, plus one DRY move.

(a) Replace the false message, which is the actual defect (main.ts:910-912). Keep a tolerance the student can read off the drawing, but state the physics in the words. Messages pass through renderMath (challengeEngine.ts:814), so author the math as LaTeX, per the repo's KaTeX-only rule:
  correct -> "On this flat, not-to-scale drawing, yes. In reality the umbra is only $0.69^{\circ}$ in angular radius at the Moon's distance, so the Moon must be within about $0.95^{\circ}$ of the antisolar point $-$ and also near an orbital node, because the lunar orbit is tilted $5.1^{\circ}$ to the ecliptic, which this 2-D model cannot show. That node condition is why lunar eclipses happen about twice a year, not every Full Moon. See Eclipse Geometry."
  incorrect -> keep "Move the Moon into the shadow cone (near Full Moon)."
Add the Eclipse Geometry link next to the feedback (index.html already links `../eclipse-geometry/` at :198-199) rather than relying on the message text, since showFeedback sets textContent.

(b) Stop the magic 30. Derive the threshold from the drawn geometry so the check and the picture cannot drift again: export the cone geometry from logic.ts (apex x = 225, tip x = 380, half-width 15 at the tip, i.e. the values currently hard-coded in the SVG path at index.html:287) and test overlap of the drawn Moon disk with the drawn umbra:
  const { x, y } = computeOrbitalPosition(normalized, ORBITAL_CENTER, ORBITAL_RADIUS);
  const half = UMBRA_HALF_WIDTH_AT_TIP * (x - UMBRA_APEX_X) / (UMBRA_TIP_X - UMBRA_APEX_X);
  const inShadowZone = x > UMBRA_APEX_X && Math.abs(y - ORBITAL_CENTER.y) <= half + MOON_RADIUS;
That accepts roughly |alpha| <= 11 deg, matches what is drawn, and is driven by the same constants the drawing uses. Drive the SVG path from those exported constants too (or at minimum assert the path against them in logic.test.ts) so index.html stops being a second source of truth for the cone.

(c) While there: the drawn umbra diverges away from Earth (index.html:287), but the real umbra converges to a point at ~1.38e6 km, about 3.6 lunar distances. Either converge the path or label it "schematic, not to scale" in the cone's existing caption (index.html:304-306) so the exaggeration is declared rather than implied.

Do not apply `normalized < 1 || normalized > 359` on its own: with MOON_RADIUS = 15 on ORBITAL_RADIUS = 120 the drawn Moon subtends 7.1 deg, so a $\pm 1^{\circ}$ check is unreadable from the figure and would reject a Moon drawn squarely inside the cone.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED, with one framing correction and a fix objection.

1. Code exists verbatim. `apps/demos/src/demos/moon-phases/main.ts:906`: `const inShadowZone = normalized < 30 || normalized > 330;` and :910-912 `message: inShadowZone ? "Yes — that’s a lunar eclipse alignment." : "Move the Moon into the shadow cone (near Full Moon)."`. `normalized = normalizeAngle(angleDeg)` (:905), and the convention is confirmed at main.ts:960 and index.html:100-101: alpha = Sun-Moon-Earth phase angle, 0 = Full, 180 = New. In the 2-D model the Moon's angular separation from the antisolar point as seen from Earth IS alpha, so the check is a +/-30 deg window about the eclipse axis.

2. Independent recomputation (my own `node -e`, R_earth = 6378 km, R_sun = 695700 km, R_moon = 1737.4 km, d_moon = 384400 km, d_sun = 1.495978707e8 km):
   R_umbra(d_moon) = 6378 - (695700-6378)(384400/1.49598e8) = 4606.7 km; angular radius atan(4606.7/384400) = 0.6866 deg.
   Moon angular radius = atan(1737.4/384400) = 0.2590 deg.
   Partial umbral contact: +/-0.9456 deg. Total umbral: +/-0.4277 deg. Any penumbral contact: R_pen = 8149.3 km -> +/-1.4734 deg.
   30/0.9456 = 31.7x too wide against the umbra; 30/1.4734 = 20.4x too wide even against the penumbra. The finder's arithmetic reproduces.
   Readout at alpha = 29: f = (1+cos 29)/2 = 0.937 -> "94%" (logic.ts:252, Math.round), and PHASE_BINS in packages/physics/src/moonPhasesModel.ts:4-5 puts 22.5-67.5 in "Waning Gibbous". So "Waning Gibbous, 94% illuminated" next to "that's a lunar eclipse alignment" is exact.

3. It also contradicts its own drawing, which the finding understates. The umbra cone is a hard-coded static path, index.html:287 `M 225 200 L 380 185 L 380 215 Z`: apex at Earth's limb (Earth at ORBITAL_CENTER (200,200), r=25), half-angle atan(15/155) = 5.53 deg; penumbra (index.html:294) 12.88 deg. With ORBITAL_RADIUS = 120 and MOON_RADIUS = 15 (logic.ts:10-13) and moon position x = 200+120cos a, y = 200-120sin a (logic.ts:175-185, +x = antisolar, Sun at cx=-60, sunlight arrows -> +x): the drawn Moon's disk still overlaps the drawn umbra out to ~11 deg and the drawn penumbra out to ~17 deg, but at alpha = 20 it clears both (|dy| = 41.0 vs umbra half-width 8.5 + 15, pen 20.1 + 15) and at alpha = 29 |dy| = 58.2, a ~35 unit gap. So ~18-30 deg (and mirrored) is a band where the student is told "Yes" while the Moon is visibly clear of both cones. The check is calibrated to nothing: not the physics (+/-0.95 deg), not the drawn umbra (5.53 deg half-angle), not the penumbra.

4. Reachable and live. #btn-challenges is a visible toolbar button (index.html:41-45) wired at main.ts:182-185/871-880; slider is min 0 max 360 step 1 (index.html:93-97); snap is only +/-2 deg to cardinals (logic.ts:8, SNAP_DEGREES = 2) so 20-29 deg is freely reachable by slider, drag or arrow keys (5 deg steps). No upstream guard: grep for inShadowZone shows the single site. `git log -5 -- .../main.ts` (latest 4351045) shows no fix. Worse than claimed: the challenge's own `initialState: { showShadow: true, angleDeg: 10 }` (main.ts:895) already satisfies the check at launch, and this is the LAST challenge, so ChallengeEngine prints "Correct! Yes - that's a lunar eclipse alignment." (challengeEngine.ts:423, 799-815) and then runs complete() after 1500 ms - the false claim is the closing line of the whole challenge set.

5. Severity stands at P0: a reader-visible assertion of wrong physics on the single point this demo exists to teach (its declared misconception is "Phases are caused by Earth's shadow", moon-phases.md:19), manufacturing a new misconception (eclipses over ~1/6 of each synodic month). Mitigating but not exculpating: the demo is `status: beta` / `readiness: candidate` (moon-phases.md:3,10), so this is not additionally a readiness-honesty violation.

6. The proposed fix is wrong in its first half. `normalized < 1 || normalized > 359` makes the check 25x tighter than the picture it tells the student to read: the drawn Moon's own angular radius is atan(15/120) = 7.1 deg, so at alpha = 1.4 deg (reachable by drag, which is continuous - main.ts:534-546) the Moon sits dead-centre in the cone, reads "Full Moon, 100%", and the demo would answer "Move the Moon into the shadow cone". Fix the false claim, not the tolerance.

findings.title: Reader copy calls the 0-360 deg slider alpha the "Sun-Moon-Earth phase angle"; that angle is bounded 0-180 deg, so every value above 180 is mislabeled (alpha=294 -> true i=66 deg)
findings.evidence: index.html:74 "Phase angle α (deg)", :85 "We use α as the Sun–Moon–Earth phase angle", :100 "In this model: α = Sun–Moon–Earth angle", main.ts:977 "Angle $\\alpha$ is the Sun–Moon–Earth phase angle in this model", exportPayload.ts:41 "Phase angle alpha (deg)". The Sun-Moon-Earth angle (vertex at the Moon) is bounded 0-180 deg by definition. I recomputed the true value from the demo's own elongation relation, elongation = (alpha - 180) mod 360: alpha=294 -> elongation 114 -> Sun-Moon-Earth angle 66 deg; alpha=315 -> 45 deg; alpha=203 -> 157 deg. The readout strip shows "Angle 294 deg" under that name. Meanwhile index.html:555 calls the same symbol "the Sun-Earth-Moon phase angle" (vertex at Earth = the elongation, a different angle), and moon-phases.md:17 says "Sun–Earth–Moon geometry" while :28 says "Sun–Moon–Earth".
findings.scenario: A student copies "alpha = Sun-Moon-Earth angle = 294 deg" into a lab notebook, or into the Station Mode table whose column header is "Phase angle alpha (deg)". On the next problem set, asked for the Sun-Moon-Earth angle of a waxing gibbous Moon, they answer 294 deg instead of 66 deg, and they cannot reconcile the demo's definition with the textbook's 0-180 phase angle.
findings.fix:
Fix the copy only; leave the physics API alone (nothing computed is wrong, and `f=(1+\cos\alpha)/2` is even in alpha).

1. Rename the quantity in reader-visible text to an orbital-position name, not a second "phase angle": `index.html:74` -> "Orbital position $\alpha$ from Full Moon (deg)"; `index.html:100` -> "In this model: $\alpha$ = position around the orbit, measured from Full Moon"; `index.html:85` tooltip -> "$\alpha$ measures the Moon's position around its orbit from Full Moon; it sets the lit fraction via $f = (1+\cos\alpha)/2$."; `main.ts:977` -> same wording. Keep `index.html:101` ("0 deg = Full, 180 deg = New") as is — it is already correct.
2. Add one KaTeX line to the Model notes tab (`index.html:558-561`) giving both bridges to the textbook quantities: $\text{elongation} = (\alpha - 180)\bmod 360$ (eastward, matching `riseSetModel.ts:134`) and the true phase angle $i = |180^{\circ} - \text{elongation}| = \min(\alpha,\,360^{\circ}-\alpha)$, with the worked case $\alpha = 294^{\circ} \Rightarrow i = 66^{\circ}$. That is what stops a student transcribing 294 deg as a Sun-Moon-Earth angle.
3. Fix the self-contradiction at `index.html:555`: "Sun-Earth-Moon phase angle $\alpha$" -> the same orbital-position wording.
4. Fix the two data surfaces the failure scenario actually names, which the original fix missed: `exportPayload.ts:42` and `main.ts:992`, both `"Phase angle alpha (deg)"` -> `"Orbital position alpha from Full (deg)"`. Consider adding a derived export row `"Phase angle i (deg)"` with `Math.min(normalized, 360 - normalized)` so an exported lab table carries the textbook quantity too.
5. Fix `apps/site/src/content/demos/moon-phases.md`: `:15` and `:28` must agree (use "Sun-Earth-Moon geometry" for the elongation picture and drop the "Sun-Moon-Earth" phrasing at `:28`), and `:16`/`:22`/`:35` should say "orbital position" where they now say "phase angle".

findings.title: Detector offset sign is inverted: the star's apparent position shifts WITH the Earth instead of against it, contradicting the sightlines drawn in the adjacent orbit panel
findings.evidence: `const scalar = pMas * dotVec2(earthPosAu, axis); return scaleVec2(axis, scalar);` For a star at barycentric d*u observed from b (AU), the topocentric unit vector is u' = (d*u - b)/|...| ~ u - b_perp/d, so the apparent angular offset is MINUS p*(b . axis) axis, not plus. Recomputed at three asymmetric phases for d = 10 pc (p = 100 mas), axisHat = (-1,0): phase 37 deg, r.axis = -0.7986 AU, code offset along axis = -79.864 mas, correct = +79.864 mas; phase 143 deg, code = +79.864, correct = -79.864; phase 251 deg, code = +32.557, correct = -32.557. Cross-checked against the geometry the demo itself draws: the unit sightline Earth->star in the orbit panel has sky-plane components +0.8615, -0.8615, -0.1593 at those same three phases — the same sign as the correct value and the opposite of the code's at all three.
findings.scenario: Student sets d = 10 pc, scrubs the orbit to 37 deg and compares the two panels. The left panel's amber ray from Earth to the star leans one way; the right panel's "Now" marker moves the other way. With blink mode on and captures at 0 and 180 deg the image blinks left-right in the same sense as Earth's own motion. Asked the standard exam question — "a nearby star appears to shift which way relative to the observer's motion?" — the student answers "the same way", which is backwards, and the signed readout `deltaTheta_signed` reports that wrong sign to three decimals and into the clipboard export.

2. apps/demos/src/demos/parallax-distance/logic.test.ts — the existing test at :52-65 is sign-invariant and must not be treated as coverage. findings.note:
CONFIRMED on every check; I could not refute it.

1. CODE EXISTS VERBATIM. /Users/anna/Teaching/cosmic-playground/apps/demos/src/demos/parallax-distance/logic.ts:120-129 is `detectorTrueOffsetMasFromPosition`, and line 127 is exactly `const scalar = pMas * dotVec2(earthPosAu, axis);` followed by `return scaleVec2(axis, scalar);` (line 128). The basis is fixed at main.ts:123 `buildParallaxBasis({x:0,y:1})`, so starDirHat = (0,1) and axisHat = perp = (-1,0) (logic.ts:107-108, perpVec2 at :99).

2. INDEPENDENT RECOMPUTATION (not the finder's arithmetic). I did not use the linearized -p(b.axis); I built the exact topocentric vector v = d*u - b with 1 pc = 648000/pi = 206264.806247096 AU and took the signed angle via atan2(v.axis, v.u), converted rad -> mas. For d = 10 pc (p = 100 mas), axisHat = (-1,0):
   - phase 37 deg: b.axis = -0.79864 AU; code = -79.864 mas; exact apparent offset = +79.864 mas
   - phase 143 deg: b.axis = +0.79864 AU; code = +79.864 mas; exact = -79.864 mas
   - phase 251 deg: b.axis = +0.32557 AU; code = +32.557 mas; exact = -32.557 mas
   - phase 0 deg (the DEFAULT state): code = -100 mas; exact = +100 mas
   Exactly opposite in sign at every phase. Physically: the apparent displacement is anti-parallel to the observer's sky-plane displacement (the train-window effect), so the correct offset is -p*(b.axisHat)*axisHat.

3. CROSS-PANEL CONTRADICTION IS REAL AND ALGEBRAIC, NOT COINCIDENTAL. renderOrbit (main.ts:703, 719) draws rayNow from the Earth's screen position to starPos = ORBIT_CENTER + starDirHat*148, and renderDetector (main.ts:770-784) draws its axis and markers from DETECTOR_CENTER along the SAME `state.axisHat`, in the same unflipped screen frame (orbitToScreen main.ts:486-489, detectorToScreen main.ts:492-502). The axis-component of the drawn ray is (starDirHat*148 - b*138).axisHat = -138*(b.axisHat), since starDirHat.axisHat = 0 — i.e. it carries the sign of the CORRECT offset at every phase and every star distance. My numbers for the normalized drawn ray: +0.8615 (37 deg), -0.8615 (143 deg), -0.1593 (251 deg) — same sign as exact, opposite to code, reproducing the finder's cross-check. The detector panel is not a free-polarity abstraction: index.html:199 aria-label "live plus captured apparent positions", :234 "Background stars stay fixed while the apparent target position shifts", :282 "the target shifts against fixed background stars on the detector". It claims to be the apparent sky position, so the relative sign is observable and self-contradictory.

4. REACHABLE, UNGUARDED, NOT FIXED. `detectorNow` is set unconditionally every frame (main.ts:783-784); the orbit auto-plays (`isPlaying: !prefersReducedMotionEnabled()`, main.ts:132); d = 10 pc is the default (main.ts:125); every capture goes through the same function (main.ts:563-567, 608-612). No downstream negation: `offsetPx` (logic.ts:202-204) is sign-preserving, and the clamp at main.ts:494-498 is symmetric +/-DETECTOR_RANGE_PX. git log: the line was introduced in 709bcf6 (2026-02-08, "Redesign parallax-distance demo with capture-first inference workflow") per `git log -L 120,129`, and the only later commit touching the file (4da8a9b) left it unchanged; it is still there in the working tree. grep found no guard.

5. THE WRONG SIGN IS ALSO A PUBLISHED NUMBER. `deltaThetaSignedMas` = (offsetB - offsetA).axis (logic.ts:276) flips with the bug; it is rendered to the student at index.html:243 ("Signed: ... mas") via main.ts:894-895 and exported as "Measured signed shift deltaTheta_signed (mas)" at main.ts:1107-1109.

6. TESTS DO NOT PIN THE CORRECT SIGN (do not cite them as evidence either way). logic.test.ts:52-65 checks only phases 0/90/180 and the sign-invariant antisymmetry `at0.x ≈ -at180.x` — it passes identically under either sign. This is precisely the repo's documented trap (CLAUDE.md: "Test physics at asymmetric points, not only symmetric ones"). The inference tests (logic.test.ts:104-149) pass literal detectorMeasMas vectors and never call the offending function. The integration tests use magnitudes only (`Math.hypot` at main.integration.test.ts:76, `Math.abs(...) > 0.5` at :177, `> 0` at :189), so no existing test encodes the defect and the fix turns nothing red.

7. SEVERITY: P0 STANDS. p_hat and d_hat use |deltaTheta| (logic.ts:277, 300-301), so the headline inferred parallax and distance stay correct — but the rubric's P0 is "wrong physics/wrong number/wrong drawing a student would believe", and this is a wrong drawing in the default view plus a wrong signed number on screen and in the clipboard export. It also inverts the exact conceptual point the demo advertises (frontmatter learning_goal "Earth moves in orbit, line-of-sight changes, apparent star position shifts"; misconception "Parallax is about the star moving physically"). Aggravating, not mitigating: apps/site/src/content/demos/parallax-distance.md claims `status: stable`, `content_verified: true`, `readiness: launch-ready` with readinessReason "Physics and page checked in the September 2026 audits with nothing open" — an audit that postdates the 2026-02-08 introduction and missed it.

8. THE PROPOSED FIX WORKS AND BREAKS NOTHING. Negating line 127 leaves |offset| unchanged, so applyAxisNoiseToOffset (logic.ts:193-200), errorRadiusPx (:206-214, uses Math.abs), p_hat, d_hat, all sigmas and the SNR are untouched; only the drawn direction and deltaTheta_signed flip, both of which is the intent. I would add two things the finder left out: a cross-panel regression assertion, and moving the formula out of demo code (it is an inline physics equation, which violates the project's "all physics from @cosmic/physics" invariant — the sign convention should have one owner).

findings.title: "Days elapsed" readout reads "2.7 yr days" past day 1000: formatDays switches the value to years while the unit span is hardcoded "days" (and the export emits value "4.2 yr" under the name "Days elapsed")
findings.evidence: index.html:118 hardcodes the unit: `0 days`. main.ts:243 writes `daysElapsedReadout.textContent = formatDays(elapsedDays)`, and logic.ts:196-200 switches unit at 1000: `if (days < 1000) return Math.round(days).toString(); return (days / yearDays()).toFixed(1) + " yr";`. I reran formatDays: 999 -> "999 days" (ok); 1000 -> "2.7 yr days"; 1500 -> "4.1 yr days"; 2329 -> "6.4 yr days". At the slider's default 10 days/s this appears after 100 s; at max 100 days/s after 10 s. The first Mars alignment is at day 769 and the second at 1549, so any student who watches two events sees it.
findings.scenario: Student selects Mars, leaves the default speed, waits 100 s to catch the second opposition. The readout reads "4.1 yr days" and later "6.4 yr days". A student asked to measure the interval between alignments reads 6.4 and 4.1 as day counts, computes 2.3 days between oppositions, and concludes the synodic period is 2.3 days against the 779.9 shown one row above.
findings.fix: The root cause is two authorities for one quantity's unit: a static unit span in index.html:118 and a unit suffix baked into the value string by logic.ts:196-200. Collapse it to one. Preferred (smallest, and best for the demo's teaching task): drop the year branch and always report days. The synodic period one row above is in days (index.html:114), and the exercise is comparing the elapsed interval to it, so the value must stay in the same unit — logic.ts becomes `return Math.round(days).toString();` after the finite guard. The static "days" span is then true for every value, the aria announcement at main.ts:209 already agrees, and the export row needs no change. This requires updating logic.test.ts:269-273, which currently asserts the years behavior — that test pins the defect and should be replaced with one asserting a plain day count at, say, 1549 d -> "1549". If a year readout is wanted for large elapsed times (a display-convention call for Anna, not mine): have one helper return the pair, e.g. `formatElapsed(days): { value: string; unit: "days" | "yr" }`, give the unit span an id (`days` — keep the class, since design-contracts.test.ts:79 matches on `class="cp-readout__unit"` and requires >= 5 of them), and set both spans from that one return in main.ts:243. Do NOT fix only the readout: main.ts:372 must take the same pair and emit a unit-homogeneous row (`{ name: "Days elapsed (days)", value: }`, or name/value/unit as three fields), otherwise the export keeps shipping "4.2 yr" under a name that says days — the half that survives into a student's lab writeup with no visible "yr days" to warn them. The finder's proposed fix is sound; I would additionally insist on the logic.test.ts change, since leaving those assertions in place either blocks the fix or re-pins the old behavior.

Correction to the finding: alignment 2 reads "4.2 yr days", not "4.1 yr days" ("4.1 yr" is day 1500, reachable but not an event instant). The defect is unchanged. 3. Reachable with no interaction at all. elapsedDays is a free-running accumulator (main.ts:117 init, main.ts:266 `elapsedDays += dtSec * speed`), never clamped or wrapped; only Reset zeroes it (main.ts:292). Speed slider is min 1 / max 100 / default 10 d per real second (index.html:38). 1000 d arrives after 1000/10 = 100 s of real time on defaults, or 10 s at max; the 2nd Mars alignment at 155 s on defaults. No control need be touched. 4. Not fixed and not guarded elsewhere. `git status --porcelain` on the demo dir is clean; `git log -3` on index.html/main.ts/logic.ts ends at 832cb7d (opposition/inferior-conjunction labelling), which did not touch the unit. The shipped artifact carries it too: apps/site/public/play/planetary-conjunctions/index.html still contains `id="daysElapsed">0 days`. 5. Severity corrected P0 -> P1. No number is wrong: 4.2 yr is 1549 d correctly converted. The unit text beside it is wrong, and it is visibly wrong — "4.2 yr days" announces itself as a bug rather than passing as a credible day count, so the finder's scenario (reading 6.4 and 4.1 as days and deducing a 2.3-day synodic period against the 779.9 shown one row above) requires the student to ignore the "yr" they have just read. Under this audit's rubric that lands on P1, not P0: it is a readout-contract violation plus misleading copy, in a demo honestly marked `status: draft` / `readiness: experimental` (apps/site/src/content/demos/planetary-conjunctions.md:3,10). The real pedagogical damage is still P1-sized: the demo's measurement task is comparing the interval between alignments to P_syn in days, and past day 1000 the readout silently stops reporting days, changes unit mid-experiment, and contradicts both its own static label "Days elapsed" and the aria announcement at main.ts:209, which keeps reporting raw days ("Opposition 2 at day 1549"). So the screen-reader path says 1549 days while the visual path says "4.2 yr days". 6. Related defects worth noting. The export at main.ts:372 `{ name: "Days elapsed", value: formatDays(elapsedDays) }` is the half where the contradiction becomes machine-readable: a row whose name declares days and whose value is the string "4.2 yr", which lands as text in a column a student or grader may read numerically. Also, logic.test.ts:269-273 pins the broken behavior (`expect(formatDays(1460)).toMatch(/yr/)` and `toContain("4.0")`), and design-contracts.test.ts:78-81 asserts only that >= 5 `class="cp-readout__unit"` spans EXIST — the very static-span pattern that makes the defect possible — so both suites stay green over it. Another instance of this repo's "tests encode the defect" pattern.

findings.title: Alignments are announced at the 5 deg threshold instead of at the alignment, so the event day is 1.39% of P_syn early (Mars: "day 769" against the demo's own 779.9 d readout); the interval between two announced events is correct
findings.evidence: main.ts:200-211 counts on the rising edge of the threshold, not at the alignment: `const sepDeg = angularSeparationDeg(earthAngle, targetAngle); const inConj = isConjunction(sepDeg, CONJUNCTION_THRESHOLD_DEG); if (inConj && !lastWasConjunction && elapsedDays > 1) { conjunctionCount++; ... setLiveRegionText(status, `${alignmentLabel(...)} ${conjunctionCount} at day ${Math.round(elapsedDays)}.`) }`. The edge fires when separation first falls to 5 deg, which is 5/(360/P_syn) days before separation reaches 0. I reimplemented the exact detector in node and stepped it at 60 fps: Mars events at days 769.2, 1549.0, 2329.0 against true alignments at 779.9, 1559.8, 2339.7 (lead 10.8 d); Venus 575.8 vs 583.9 (lead 8.1 d); Jupiter 393.3 vs 398.9 (5.5 d); Saturn 373.0 vs 378.1 (5.3 d). The lead is 5/360 = 1.389% of P_syn for every target. Because both bodies also start at longitude 0 (an alignment at t=0 that is deliberately not counted), the elapsed day of the first announced event is the student's measured first interval.
findings.scenario: Student follows the exhibit's own play_steps ("Measure the time between two conjunctions"), starts at day 0 with the bodies aligned on screen, and hears "Opposition 1 at day 769". The readout immediately above says the synodic period is 779.9 days. The two numbers the demo gives for the same quantity disagree by 11 days, with nothing on the page to explain the gap, so the student either distrusts the model or records 769 d as the Earth-Mars synodic period.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED, with a severity correction.

1) Code exists as quoted. apps/demos/src/demos/planetary-conjunctions/main.ts:200-212 is verbatim: `const sepDeg = angularSeparationDeg(earthAngle, targetAngle);` (200), `const inConj = isConjunction(sepDeg, CONJUNCTION_THRESHOLD_DEG);` (201), `if (inConj && !lastWasConjunction && elapsedDays > 1) {` (204), `conjunctionCount++` (205), the `setLiveRegionText(... at day ${Math.round(elapsedDays)}.)` (209), `lastWasConjunction = inConj;` (212). `CONJUNCTION_THRESHOLD_DEG = 5` at main.ts:110. `isConjunction` is a bare `separationDeg <= thresholdDeg` (logic.ts:121-124), so the branch fires on the first frame separation falls to 5 deg, not at the alignment.

2) Independent recomputation (my own chain from the source constants, not the finder's). Periods from RetrogradeMotionModel.planetElements (retrogradeMotionModel.ts:37-41), P_yr = sqrt(a^3/M) (twoBodyAnalytic.ts:89-94), yearDays = 31557600/86400 = 365.25 (logic.ts:66-68), P_syn = |P1*P2/(P1-P2)| (twoBodyAnalytic.ts:285-291):
  P_Earth = 365.2514 d; P_Mars = 686.980 d -> P_syn = 779.914 d; Venus 583.918 d; Jupiter 398.860 d; Saturn 378.090 d.
Re-simulating the exact detector at 60 fps, speed 10 d/s (slider default, index.html:38):
  Mars events at days 769.17, 1549.00, 2329.00 vs true alignments 779.91, 1559.83, 2339.74 -> lead 10.75, 10.83, 10.74 d
  Venus 575.83 vs 583.92 (lead 8.08 d); Jupiter 393.33 vs 398.86 (5.53 d); Saturn 373.00 vs 378.09 (5.09 d)
Analytic lead = (5 deg)/(360 deg/P_syn) = 5/360 = 1.3889% of P_syn = 10.83 d for Mars. My measured leads are 1.35-1.39% (just under the analytic value because the edge fires on the first frame already inside 5 deg). This reproduces the finder's numbers; their Saturn figure of 5.3 d is 5.09-5.18 d in my run, an immaterial difference.

3) Reachable. Default target is Mars (`selectPlanet("Mars")`, main.ts:406), the loop autostarts (main.ts:407), and the announcement goes to `#status`, which is `role="status" aria-live="polite"` (index.html:69), so it reaches sighted and screen-reader students alike. `formatNumber(synPeriodDays, 1)` renders 779.914 -> "779.9" in the Synodic period readout (index.html:112), so the two conflicting numbers are on screen together. Not clamped or guarded anywhere. I also checked the worst case (speed 100 -> step 1.667 d): the window half-width is 5.25-10.83 d for all four presets, so the window is never stepped over and the lead persists (Mars 9.9 d).

4) Not already fixed. `git log` on main.ts: last touch is 832cb7d, which fixed the opposition/conjunction *label*, not the timing. No `minSep`/`interpolat`/`closestApproach`/latch guard anywhere in the demo or in twoBodyAnalytic.ts. logic.test.ts asserts only the pure predicate (`isConjunction(5,5) === true`, lines 199-217) and the label classification (lines 367-427); no assertion touches the announced day, so nothing pins or excuses this.

5) Severity corrected P0 -> P1. What is genuinely wrong: the announced event day. What the finder's failure scenario overstates: the interval. Both events carry the same offset, so the gap between two *announced* events is P_syn to within one frame step - I measured 779.833 d vs 779.914 (Mars) and 584.000 vs 583.918 (Venus). The exhibit's learning goal ("estimate the time between successive conjunctions", planetary-conjunctions.md:17) and its play step ("Measure the time between two conjunctions", line 24, quoted correctly) therefore come out right. The error only bites the student who anchors on day 0, which is a real trap: both bodies start at longitude 0 (`planetAngleRad(0,P) = 0`, logic.ts:93-101), `inConj` is true at t=0 so the alignment ray IS drawn (main.ts:215) while `elapsedDays > 1` suppresses the count, so the student sees an unlabelled alignment at day 0 and then hears "day 769". Mitigating further: the model itself is exact (P_syn, periods and both longitude readouts are correct) - this is an annunciator defect, not wrong physics - and the demo makes no quality claim it cannot back: planetary-conjunctions.md:3,4,10 are `status: draft`, `content_verified: false`, `readiness: experimental`, so the exhibit carries the "Active development" callout and the card the readiness badge. A wrong number a student would read, but not a wrong model and not the measurement the exhibit asks for: P1.

6) The proposed fix would work but is the weaker of its two variants and more machinery than this case needs. "Latch the minimum and announce on window exit" gives the right day but delays the announcement ~10.8 d of sim time past the event, desyncing the flash from the alignment. The signed-wrap-plus-interpolation variant is correct but unnecessary here: for coplanar circular orbits both starting at longitude 0, alignments are exactly at t = k*P_syn (lambda_E = lambda_T mod 2pi <=> t(1/P_E - 1/P_T) = k), which I verified numerically - separation at k*P_syn is 0 to 1e-13 deg for all four presets, k = 1,2,3. So the crossing time is analytic and needs no interpolation.

findings.title: Lambda arc overlay sweeps 360 - lambda, and reverses sense, whenever lambda_app > 180 deg
findings.evidence: `orbitToPx` (main.ts:807-812) returns screen `y = centerY - yAu*scale`, so `dy` at main.ts:998 is already screen-space and equals -(dyAu*scale). main.ts:1015 then takes `const angle = Math.atan2(dy, dx)`, i.e. the NEGATED ecliptic longitude, and `arcPathFromAngles` (main.ts:814-830) sets `largeArcFlag = Math.abs(delta) > Math.PI ? 1 : 0`. Because `Math.atan2` returns (-pi, pi], |delta| never exceeds pi, so largeArcFlag is always 0 and the arc always takes the short way round. I recomputed the drawn sweep against the readout in node: lambda_app = 45 -> arc 45.0 deg (error 0); 135 -> 135.0 (0); 200 -> 160.0 (error -40 deg); 300 -> 60.0 (error -240 deg); 359 -> 1.0 (error -358 deg). The arc ends on the correct ray, so only the swept magnitude is wrong - for exactly half of every orbit.
findings.scenario: A student checks "Show lambda angle arc" to see what lambda_app means, scrubs to a day where the lambda readout reads 300.0 deg, and sees an arc labeled lambda_app subtending 60 deg. They conclude either that lambda is measured the other way round or that the readout is wrong. This is the only overlay in the demo whose job is to define lambda, and for half the window it defines it wrong.
findings.fix:
Hand `arcPathFromAngles` the true sweep and leave the helper alone (its `largeArcFlag`/`sweepFlag` logic is already correct for any |delta| < 2pi — verified by solving the rendered centre from the path data).

In main.ts:1014-1042, stop recomputing the geometry inline and reuse the model value that is already wrapped to [0,360). `currentDisplayState` is module-level (assigned at main.ts:500), so inside `renderOrbitDynamic` (main.ts:928):

  const lambdaDeg = currentDisplayState?.lambdaDeg;
  if (state.showLambdaArc && dist > 0.01 && Number.isFinite(lambdaDeg)) {
    const lambdaRad = (lambdaDeg * Math.PI) / 180;   // already in [0, 2pi)
    const endAngleRad = -lambdaRad;                  // screen y points down
    ... arcPathFromAngles({ cx: observerPx.x, cy: observerPx.y, radius: arcRadius,
                            startAngleRad: 0, endAngleRad }) ...

I verified this end to end: rendered swept angle equals lambda_app to 1e-3 deg across 45/135/179/180/181/200/270/300/359, largeArcFlag correctly becomes 1 past 180 deg, sweepFlag stays 0 (physically lambda-increasing) across the whole range, and the solved arc centre stays exactly on the observer dot. If you prefer not to depend on `currentDisplayState`, the equivalent local form is `const lambdaRad = ((Math.atan2(-dy, dx) % (2*Math.PI)) + 2*Math.PI) % (2*Math.PI);` — the wrap is the load-bearing part the original fix omitted.

Two changes the original fix missed:
1. main.ts:1034 must move with it: `const midAngle = -lambdaRad / 2;` (the old `angle * 0.5` puts the label off the drawn arc for lambda > 180 — e.g. label at screen +30 deg while the arc midpoint is at -150 deg for lambda = 300).
2. Guard lambda_app = 0 exactly: start and end coincide, so the `A` command degenerates and nothing renders. That is the correct result for a zero angle, but add the explicit `lambdaRad > 1e-6` condition rather than relying on it.

Worth doing in the same edit: put the numeric value in the arc label so the drawing is cross-checkable against `#readoutLambda`, and render it with `renderMath()` from `@cosmic/runtime` — the current `arcLabel.textContent = "λ_app"` (main.ts:1036) is a raw Unicode lambda in reader-visible SVG text, which the KaTeX-only invariant forbids (the exemption covers Canvas 2D / uPlot only, not SVG). Also add a contract test asserting the emitted path's `largeArcFlag` is 1 for a day whose lambda_app exceeds 180 deg — there is currently no test anywhere touching this overlay.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED — the code exists as quoted and I reproduced the defect independently.

1. Code exists verbatim. `orbitToPx` at main.ts:807-812 returns `y: context.centerY - yAu * context.scale` (screen, y down). main.ts:997-998 forms `dx/dy` from those screen points, so `dy = -(dyAu*scale)`. main.ts:1014 is `if (state.showLambdaArc && dist > 0.01) {` and main.ts:1015 is exactly `const angle = Math.atan2(dy, dx);`, passed as `endAngleRad` with `startAngleRad: 0` at main.ts:1019-1026. `arcPathFromAngles` is at main.ts:814-830 with `const largeArcFlag = Math.abs(delta) > Math.PI ? 1 : 0;` at main.ts:827.

2. Independent recomputation (I did NOT reuse the finder's arithmetic). I copied `arcPathFromAngles` faithfully, then decided the rendered arc from the emitted path data using my own SVG F.6.5/F.6.6 endpoint-to-center solver, with a center-identity assertion (`centerOk: true` for every case, so the arc really is the one centred on the observer dot). Rendered swept angle vs. the lambda the readout shows, in degrees:
  lambda_app = 45 -> 45.000 (err 0); 135 -> 135.000 (0); 180 -> 180.000 (0); 200 -> 160.000 (err -40 deg); 270 -> 90.000 (-180 deg); 300 -> 60.000 (-240 deg); 359 -> 1.000 (-358 deg).
Matches the finder's numbers. Mechanism as claimed: `angle` = -lambda_principal, `Math.atan2` returns (-pi, pi], so |delta| <= pi, largeArcFlag is always 0. Two visible symptoms, not one: the magnitude becomes min(lambda, 360-lambda), AND `sweepFlag` flips from 0 to 1 at lambda = 180, so past 180 deg the arc also sweeps in the physically lambda-DECREASING sense. The terminal ray is correct (I confirmed the end ray lands on physical longitude 200/270/300/359 deg respectively), so only the swept arc is wrong.

3. Reachable. The control is a live checkbox, `#showLambdaArc` (index.html:127-128, "Show lambda angle arc"), bound at main.ts:86/197 and main.ts:1315-1316; no `checked` attribute, so opt-in. `dist > 0.01` is satisfied essentially always. The readout it contradicts is `#readoutLambda` (index.html:330-331), fed by `formatNumber(ds.lambdaDeg, 1)` at main.ts:503, and the model wraps to [0,360) via `wrap0To360Deg` (packages/physics/src/retrogradeMotionModel.ts:246-247), so the readout does span 180-360. I measured the exposure: coplanar circular Earth (1 AU, 1 yr) -> Mars (1.524 AU, 1.881 yr), 1-day steps over 688 days, lambda_app > 180 deg on 335 of 688 days = 48.7%. "Half of every orbit" is accurate. No upstream wrap/normalize guard exists near main.ts:1015.

4. Not already fixed. `git status --porcelain` on this file is empty, so HEAD equals the working tree; the last three commits (0f75490 Biome, 6d65b2a "Upgrade retrograde demo UX...", 8da3115 "Review retrograde motion fixes") left line 1015 as-is.

5. Severity corrected P0 -> P1. Real and reader-visible, but P0 overstates it: (a) the overlay is opt-in and off by default; (b) the arc carries no number, only the text "lambda_app", so it misrepresents the definition visually rather than asserting a wrong value; (c) the correct value is printed in the adjacent readout, so the student meets a visible contradiction rather than silent wrongness; (d) the physics model, the lambda readout, the unwrapped series and the retrograde/stationary determination are all unaffected; (e) apps/site/src/content/demos/retrograde-motion.md declares `status: draft`, `readiness: experimental`, readinessReason "Core demo behavior is implemented, but parity and launch-gate signoff are still pending" — so this is not a launch-ready public quality claim. It is still a genuine defect in the one overlay whose stated job is to define the demo's central quantity, so it is squarely P1, not P2.

6. The proposed fix does NOT work as written — I tested it. `const lambdaRad = Math.atan2(-dy, dx)` returns (-pi, pi], so the proposed test `lambdaRad > Math.PI ? 1 : 0` is dead for exactly the same reason the original is: I ran it and got lambda 45 -> 45, 200 -> 160, 300 -> 60, 359 -> 1, i.e. byte-for-byte the buggy output. The missing step is wrapping to [0, 2pi) BEFORE negating. The finder's accompanying suggestion to change `largeArcFlag` inside `arcPathFromAngles` is also wrong and unnecessary: `Math.abs(delta) > Math.PI` is already correct for any |delta| < 2pi (I verified the solved centre stays on the observer for largeArc=1 cases), and the finder's own closing sentence ("arcPathFromAngles itself is fine once it is handed the true sweep") contradicts the edit they propose. It is the only caller (main.ts:1020), so no other caller is at risk either way. The finder also missed that main.ts:1034 `const midAngle = angle * 0.5` must move with the fix: for lambda = 300 the corrected arc's midpoint is at screen -150 deg while the old formula puts the "lambda_app" label at +30 deg, i.e. off the drawn arc entirely.

findings.title: Day/night arc is built from the superseded latitude projection, so the amber daylight arc overruns the terminator by up to 39% of the globe radius
findings.evidence: dayLengthArcGeometry calls `const band = latitudeBandEllipse(latitudeDeg, tiltDeg, 0, 0, globeRadius)` (logic.ts:522) and main.ts:612-617 passes `tiltDeg: tiltVal` (the fixed obliquity), while the latitude bands the arc annotates are drawn with `projectLatitudeCircle(latDeg, dec, view=20, GLOBE_R)` (main.ts:581-595). I recomputed both ellipses for R=155. June solstice, lat 40 N, dec=23.498: band = {cx=-39.73, cy=-85.86, rx=118.74, ry=37.24, rot=-24.8 deg}; arc ellipse = {cx=0.00, cy=-91.37, rx=118.74, ry=47.35, rot=0}. Offset = 39.73 px in cx (26% of the globe radius), 10.10 px in ry, 24.8 deg of rotation the arc does not have (dayLengthArcGeometry hardcodes the SVG x-axis-rotation parameter as `0`). Worse, the terminator is the line x=0 by the demo's own construction (main.ts:566-575, night is x>0): with dayFraction = 14.853/24 = 0.6189 the arc's endpoints come out at x = +43.32 px, i.e. 43 px inside the night hemisphere. Under the correct projection the same parameter angle gives x = -39.73 + 108.95*cos(68.6 deg) = +0.01 px, on the terminator. The day fraction itself is right (I confirmed cos u = tan(lat)tan(dec) = 0.3648 -> u = +/-68.6 deg -> lit span 222.8 deg = 0.6189), so the arc's angular extent is correct and only the ellipse is wrong. At tilt = 0 (the demo's headline experiment) latitudeBandEllipse returns ry = 0, so the arc collapses to a flat line at cy=-99.63 while the band is an ellipse at cy=-93.62 with ry=40.61.
findings.scenario: Student clicks "Jun solstice", sets latitude to 40 N, reads "14h 51m" in the readout strip, then looks at the globe: the amber day arc is detached from the 40 N latitude band and its right-hand end sits 43 px inside the shaded night half, so the drawing says the Sun is up on the night side of the terminator. Setting tilt to 0 flattens the arc into a straight line that lies below the equator band entirely.
findings.fix:
Make the arc use the single convention established in 8fcedd6, and cover the degenerate branches the original proposal missed.

1. Change the signature of `dayLengthArcGeometry` (apps/demos/src/demos/seasons/logic.ts:513-519) from `tiltDeg` to `declinationDeg` plus `viewElevationDeg`, and update the only caller (apps/demos/src/demos/seasons/main.ts:612-617) to pass `declinationDeg: dec` and `viewElevationDeg: view` — not `tiltDeg: tiltVal`.

2. Inside it, replace the `latitudeBandEllipse` call (logic.ts:522) with `projectLatitudeCircle(latitudeDeg, declinationDeg, viewElevationDeg, globeRadius)` and rebuild the screen-space map locally from the same quantities that function uses: `r = globeRadius*cos(lat)`, `m00 = r*cos(dec)`, `m10 = r*sin(dec)*cos(view)`, `m11 = -r*sin(view)`, centre `(cx, cyMath) = (-globeRadius*sin(lat)*sin(dec), globeRadius*sin(lat)*cos(dec)*cos(view))`. Evaluate endpoints directly in screen coordinates:
   x(u) = cx + m00*cos(u)
   y(u) = -(cyMath + m10*cos(u) + m11*sin(u))
   at u = PI - dayFraction*PI and u = PI + dayFraction*PI.

3. Emit the A command with the projected ellipse's `rx`, `ry` and `rotationDeg` as the x-axis-rotation (replacing the hardcoded `0` at logic.ts:555 and 560). Keep `largeArcDay = dayFraction > 0.5`, `largeArcNight = dayFraction < 0.5` and sweep = 1 unchanged — the screen map is orientation-preserving (det = +R^2 cos^2(lat) cos(dec) sin(view) > 0) and the SVD's right-singular rotation is rigid, so the swept parameter span is still 2*PI*dayFraction.

4. Rebuild the two degenerate branches as well (logic.ts:526-539). Polar day and polar night are reachable (lat 70, day 172 gives 24.0 h), and both currently emit a full ellipse at cx = 0 with no rotation — 58 px off in cx at lat 70, dec 23.5. Emit the full ellipse at the projected `cx`, `cy` with the projected `rx`, `ry` and `rotationDeg`, as two half-arcs from (cx - rx', cy') to (cx + rx', cy') in the rotated frame, or simply hand main.ts the projected ellipse parameters and let it set an `<ellipse>` + rotate transform for that case, exactly as `setBand` already does.

5. Delete `latitudeBandEllipse` (logic.ts:277-300) and its nine tests (logic.test.ts:348-390). After step 2 it has no production consumer, and commit 8fcedd6 already recorded that its geometry is wrong; leaving it in place is how this defect survived.

6. Add tests that pin the physics, not the implementation. At minimum: for several asymmetric (lat, dec) pairs — (40, 23.5), (-40, 23.5), (65, 23.5), (23, -10), (55, 18) — parse both endpoints out of `dayArcD` and assert |x| < 0.05 px, i.e. both ends land on the terminator x = 0. Assert the observer marker from `projectObserverMarker` satisfies ((x-cx)/rx)^2 + ((y-cy)/ry)^2 = 1 within tolerance in the arc's own rotated frame. Assert the lit midpoint x(PI) is strictly negative (sun side). Assert the polar-day ellipse centre equals `projectLatitudeCircle`'s cx/cy. And assert that at tilt = 0 the arc is a non-degenerate ellipse with ry = globeRadius*cos(lat)*sin(view) rather than the current vanishing path.
findings.note:
CONFIRMED, and the repo's own git history proves it was a half-finished migration.

1. Code exists as quoted. `apps/demos/src/demos/seasons/logic.ts:522` is exactly `const band = latitudeBandEllipse(latitudeDeg, tiltDeg, 0, 0, globeRadius);`, inside `dayLengthArcGeometry` (logic.ts:513-563). `main.ts:612-617` passes `tiltDeg: tiltVal` where `tiltVal = args.axialTiltDeg` (main.ts:562) — the obliquity slider, not the declination. The bands use the other projection: `main.ts:582` `projectLatitudeCircle(latDeg, dec, view, GLOBE_R)` with a per-band `transform="rotate(...)"` (main.ts:583-588). The arc path never gets a transform; only `d` is set (main.ts:618-619). `latitudeBandEllipse` returns `{cy, rx, ry}` only — no cx, no rotation — and the arc's `px(a) = rx*cos(a)` (logic.ts:546) therefore pins the arc's centre at x = 0 with zero rotation and the A-command's x-axis-rotation hardcoded `0` (logic.ts:555, 560).

2. Independent recomputation (my own `node -e`, R = GLOBE_R = 155 px, view = 20 deg). Jun-solstice preset = day 172 (main.ts:1047); with eps = 23.5 the model gives dec = +23.498 deg.
   - `projectLatitudeCircle(40, 23.498, 20, 155)` = {cx = -39.725, cy = -85.860, rx = 118.737, ry = 37.243, rot = -24.829 deg}.
   - `latitudeBandEllipse(40, 23.5, 0, 0, 155)` = {cy = -91.410, rx = 118.737, ry = 47.232}. (The finder used tilt = dec = 23.498 and got cy = -91.370, ry = 47.342; main.ts actually passes the slider obliquity. Immaterial — the endpoint error below is independent of ry.)
   - Day fraction: tan(40)tan(23.498) = 0.36482, u0 = acos(0.36482) = 68.604 deg, lit fraction = 1 - 68.604/180 = 0.61887 -> 14.853 h = 14h 51m. The readout number is right; only the drawing is wrong.
   - Coded arc endpoints: x = rx*cos(pi - 0.61887*pi) = 118.737*cos(68.604 deg) = +43.32 px (both ends; y = -47.43 and -135.39 px).
   - Correct endpoints under the live map: x(u) = cx + m00*cos(u) = -39.725 + 108.891*cos(u); at u = u0 and u = 2pi - u0 this gives x = 0.0000 px and -0.0000 px.
   So each end of the amber day arc sits **43.32 px** past the terminator, which is the line x = 0 by the demo's own construction (terminator = R-radius circle at cx = +155 clipped to the globe, main.ts:566-575, night is x > 0). 43.32/155 = **28% of the globe radius**. At lat 65 N, day 172 it is **61.08 px (39% of R)**; a full parameter scan (tilt 0-90 by 0.5, day 1-365, lat -90..90 by 1 — all slider ranges, index.html:48-65) gives a worst reachable endpoint error of **154.8 px**, essentially the whole radius.
   - Corroboration independent of the terminator: the observer marker uses the correct projection (`projectObserverMarker`, main.ts:607) and sits at u = pi/2 on the true latitude circle. For lat 40, day 172 it is at (-39.73, -45.25); substituting into the arc's ellipse gives (x/rx)^2 + ((y-cy)/ry)^2 = **1.0608**, so the arc does not pass through the marker it is supposed to belong to.

3. Reachable with no interaction beyond one click. The "Day arc" overlay is `aria-pressed="true"` at index.html:492-496, i.e. ON by default, as are "Terminator" (index.html:479-482) and "Lat. Bands". The arcs are drawn after the terminator inside the same clip group (index.html:280-293), so the amber stroke (`--cp-accent-amber`, opacity 0.7, 4 px, style.css:303-316) renders on top of the night shading. (b) At tilt = 0 exactly, `latitudeBandEllipse` returns ry = 0 and dec = 0 gives dayFraction = 0.5, so both endpoints evaluate to the same point ("0.00 -99.63"); per the SVG spec an arc with identical endpoints is omitted entirely, so the day AND night arcs **vanish** rather than flattening into a line. The screen map is diag(1,-1)*M with det = +R^2 cos^2(lat) cos(dec) sin(view) > 0 for |dec| < 90, so it is orientation-preserving, and the SVD's right-singular rotation is rigid, so the swept ellipse-parameter span is still 2*pi*dayFraction — `largeArcDay = dayFraction > 0.5` and sweep = 1 remain correct. findings.title: Bohr-atom transition arrow points inward in BOTH modes, so absorption draws the emission picture and contradicts the (correct) energy ladder on the same screen
findings.evidence: The line endpoints are fixed regardless of mode: `x1,y1` come from `fromR = compressedOrbitRadius({n: state.nUpper})` (main.ts:933-937) and `x2,y2` from `toR` (n_lower), at `arrowAngle = -Math.PI/2`, so with SVG y down the line always runs from y1 = cy - fromR to y2 = cy - toR, i.e. inward/downward toward the nucleus. The only thing mode changes is `"marker-end": state.mode === "emission" ? "url(#arrowDown)" : "url(#arrowUp)"`. Those two markers are identical: both have `d: "M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z"`, `refX: 5, refY: 5`, `markerWidth/Height: 6`, and differ only in `orient: "auto-start-reverse"` (main.ts:958) versus `orient: "auto"` (main.ts:971). Per SVG 2, `auto-start-reverse` differs from `auto` ONLY for a marker placed on a marker-start vertex; on `marker-end` the two are equivalent. So the rendered arrowhead is pixel-identical in both modes. The energy ladder, 150 lines later, does it correctly by swapping endpoints: `arrowY1 = state.mode === "emission" ? yUpper + 4 : yLower - 4` (main.ts:1126). The electron animation also flips correctly (`fromN = mode === "emission" ? nUpper : nLower`, main.ts:1710). No CSS touches the markers (grep for 'marker' in style.css returns nothing).
findings.scenario: Student clicks Absorption with n_upper = 3, n_lower = 2. The energy-level diagram on the right shows the arrow going up from n=2 to n=3 (correct: the atom absorbs a photon and the electron climbs). The Bohr atom on the left shows the arrow going from the n=3 ring inward to the n=2 ring — the emission picture. The two panels contradict each other on the same screen, and the left one teaches that absorption makes the electron fall.
findings.fix:
The finder's fix is directionally right (swap endpoints by mode; collapse to one `orient: "auto"` marker) and would resolve the defect, but I would not apply it as written, for two reasons: it leaves the same mode-swap logic duplicated inline in two places (main.ts:933-939 and main.ts:1125-1126), which is what let the two panels drift apart in the first place, and its suggested test is not anchored.

What I would apply:

1. Add one pure, exported helper in `apps/demos/src/demos/spectral-lines/logic.ts`, next to `compressedOrbitRadius` and `energyLevelY`, so both panels get their direction from a single source of truth: `transitionArrowSpan({ mode, upper, lower })` returning `{ start, end }` = `mode === "emission" ? { start: upper, end: lower } : { start: lower, end: upper }`. It is coordinate-agnostic, so the Bohr panel passes radii and the ladder passes y values.

2. In `drawBohrAtom` (main.ts:933-939), call it with `{ upper: fromR, lower: toR }` and build x1/y1 from `start`, x2/y2 from `end`. Keep `wavelengthNm`/`photonColor` (main.ts:941-942) on `nUpper`/`nLower` — the photon energy is mode-independent, and the `(fromR + toR)/2` photon-label midpoint (main.ts:983-984) is symmetric so it needs no change.

4. Refactor `drawEnergyLevels` (main.ts:1125-1126) onto the same helper with `{ upper: yUpper + 4, lower: yLower - 4 }`. Behavior-preserving there (I checked the numbers above), and it is what stops the two panels from disagreeing again.

5. Give the Bohr arrow `arrowLine.id = "bohrTransitionArrow"` before appending. Today it is the only `<line>` in `#bohrAtom` (the nucleus, orbits, and electron are all `<circle>`: main.ts:833, 846, 924), so a `#bohrAtom line` selector happens to work but only incidentally — an id makes the E2E hook contractual.

6. Tests, written RED first. Primary: a unit test in `logic.test.ts` asserting `transitionArrowSpan` swaps, i.e. that emission's `{start, end}` is exactly absorption's `{end, start}`, which fails for any implementation that ignores `mode`. findings.note:
CONFIRMED — I could not refute it; every quoted line exists as claimed and the geometry reproduces independently.

1. Code exists as quoted. `apps/demos/src/demos/spectral-lines/main.ts:933-939` computes `fromR` from `state.nUpper`, `toR` from `state.nLower`, `arrowAngle = -Math.PI/2` (line 935), and x1/y1 from `fromR`, x2/y2 from `toR`. findings.title: Readout labelled "Neutral-H proxy" reads 0.000 at 4000 K where the true neutral fraction is 1.000; the expression is a Balmer-visibility window, not a neutral fraction, and contains no Saha term despite copy claiming "ionization balance"
findings.evidence: `const coolSuppression = clamp01((temperatureK - 4500) / 3500); const hotSuppression = clamp01((17000 - temperatureK) / 8000); const neutralHydrogenFractionProxy = clamp01(coolSuppression * hotSuppression);` rendered into a readout labelled 'Neutral-H proxy' (index.html:582). I evaluated it across the 4000-20000 K slider (index.html:565): T=4000 -> neutral 0.000, balmer 0.000; T=4500 -> 0.000 / 0.000; T=6000 -> 0.429 / 0.000; T=9000 -> 1.000 / 0.311; peak balmer 0.890 at T=9880 K; T=17000 -> 0.000 / 0.000; T=20000 -> 0.000 / 0.000. Physically, at 4000 K hydrogen in a stellar atmosphere is essentially entirely neutral, so the true value of the quantity the label names is about 1.0, not 0.000 — the expression is not a neutral fraction at all but an unlabelled 'fraction that makes Balmer lines' window. The Balmer proxy additionally reads exactly 0.000 for T below about 7100 K and for all T at or above 17000 K: 6100 K of a 16000 K slider, about 38% of its own range, including every B-star temperature, where Balmer absorption is in fact strong. There is no Saha term anywhere in the function despite the panel text 'excitation + ionization balance' (index.html:587). Prior review finding SL-6 recorded the dead range and is still open.
findings.scenario: Student drags the temperature slider to 18000 K under the heading 'Why Hydrogen Dominates A Stars' and reads 'Neutral-H proxy: 0.000, Balmer strength proxy: 0.000' — concluding B stars have no hydrogen lines. Dragging to 4000 K gives the same two zeros, now also asserting that cool stars contain no neutral hydrogen.

Independent recomputation (my own re-implementation from R_H=13.598434599 eV, k_B=8.617333e-5 eV/K; dE(n=2)=10.198826 eV, dE(n=3)=12.087497 eV): T=4000 K -> neutral 0.000, balmer 0.000; T=9000 K -> neutral 1.000, balmer 0.311; T=20000 K -> neutral 0.000, balmer 0.000. CORRECTIONS to the finder's evidence (none touch the core claim):
